Equal to a dividend of over 27 per cent. OR the capital of £200,000. This result would practically be about doubled by working night and day, which will be done as soon as the sales require it. (The above estimate of £l5 8 "refit per ton is a low one, for The European Globe Company ~ave been mak- ing an actual profit of R2O, per ton.) Alter the purchase and formation of The Acme Horse Shoe Nail Coy., Limited, an important improvement in Whipple's Machine was invented bypf r. J. A. Coleman, which has been patented and acquired by the Company, except as to the United States and Canada. By this a further saving in cost of produc- tion will be affected and Mr. Coleman is now engaged for this Company. superintending the making of the Machines with his improvement. The Acme Company, there is no doubt, thus owned the simplest and at the same time the most perfect Machine for the manufacture of Horse Nails, and the Nails have been during the last three months further tested by practical far- riers all over the country, and their testimonials, too numer- ous to publish, have been always practically the same—" the beat Nail we have ever used." The Directors of the Acme Com- pany knew that the only existing manufacturer which could at all compete with the Whipple's Machines was the European Globe Nail Company, established In London, with a factory at Gothenberg, in Sweden, having a Share Capital fully paid of £loo,ooo,—being art offshoot of the very successful Globe Nail Company, of Boston, U.S A. The Globe Nail Company, of Boston, has carried on a most successful business for the last ten years, paying regular divi- dends and Its shares commanding a large premium. The Globe Nails, having received the Medal for the best Horse Pail at the Philadelphia Exhibition, were exhibited at the last French Exposition, at Faris (1878), and were awarded Two Gold Medals, one of which was given at the request of the School of Veterinary Surgeons, connected with the French Army, after a thorough trial of the Nail in actual use. Such an award was never before made for a Horse Shoe Nail, nor was the distinction of two Gold Medals obtained by any other exhibit of manufactured goods. The Nails were a centre of interest during the entire progress of the Exposition, IRA samples were distributed. The great superiority of these finished Nails over the rough hand-made Nails in general use I being at once seen and recognised, a demand for finished Nails was thus created in Europe. The Globe Company of Boston, having perfected its machine, sold, in the autumn of 1879, all its Patents and Trade Marks, except in the United States and Canada, to the European Globe Nail Company, and thus estab- lished a Company able to begin to supply the demand for finished Horse Nails In Europe. The European Globe Nall Company—who have received cer- tificates from hundreds of users of their Nails—had, on the let January last, after only one clear year's work, over 400 regular customers (wholesale merchants and large consumers), and their Nails are used by most of the Continental Armies and the Imperial and Royal Stables; and they were able even with their newly established business, to sell 12 tons per week, yielding a nett profit of about £240 per week (equal to £12,480 per annum), while the works are now haying extra machinery added to about double this output. The Directors of the Acme Company found that though they could with Whipple's Machines effect a saving of 70 per cent. in the labour of manufacture, and thus produce Nails cheaper, and certainly as good tip the European Globe Company, the latter was a strong Company, and would not give up its hold on the Trade without running a vigorous competition. The Directors of the Acme Company, with the consent of their Shareholders, therefore arranged the purchase of the whole patents, trade marks, property, business and assets of The Euro- pean Globle Company, including the Factory at Gottenberg, with the extra machinery now being added, and the ordinary stock of manufactured Nails held by that Company, and to carry this amalgamation out, The United Hone Nall Company, Limited, was formed. By this means this Company acquired a going proitable business, with a large and increaing connection, and a well-known and protected Trade Mark. The establishment of a factory to use Whipple's Machines is In progress at DI illwall, and will be worked in conjunction with the factory of The Horse Shoe Manufacturing Company, Limited. Meanwhile this Company will have about 20 tons of finished Nails per week made at the factory at Gottenberg to work the trade with, upon which a profit of £4OO per week will be at once assured. ' '

-- Mr. J. W. Cole, MIME., of 54, King William-street, E.G., (late of Bells, Lightfoot, & Co., of Newcastle-on-Tyne), a prac- tical engineer of great experience, while lately in America on the business of The Horse Shoe Manufacturing Coy., was able to see the factory of the Globe Nail Coy., in Boston (which turns out 36 tons of nails per week), and also to consult with Mr. Whipple as to the factory to be erected in England. His Report to the Directors confirms the value and success of the Whipple patent. This Company owns Whipple's patents secured for Great Britaik, France, Sweden, and Belgium, and applications are now in progress for the rest of Europe, India, and the Colonies. One third of the proceeds of any of the Patents (If sold) except the above four will have to be paid as and when received to Mr. Whipple. This Company else owns The European Globe bail Company's Patents and Trade Marks for Great Britain, France, Germany, Sweden, Norway, Den- mark, Spain, Austria, Italy, and Belgium. - - -- • - • • • - -

The Globe Patent and Trade Mari for Russia has just been disposed of to the Russian Globe Nail Company, with a capital of 600,000 Roubles, and having machinery to manufacture 12 tons of Nails per week—for 180,000 Roubles (d 18,000 in fully paid -up shares, which belong to this Company. The Directors consider this a good commencement—and they have already been offered £lO,OOO cash for the German Patents and Trade Mark, whirh they have refused. They believe that the Foreign Patents generally will:be disposed of most advantageously for this Company, and the machinery in Sweden will, after the Factory in England is in proper working order, be disposad of in connection with some of the Foreign Patents. Licenses to manufacture at a Royalty may be granted where the Patent and Trade Mark are not sold: After establishing its factory in England, and providing 40 of Whipple's machines to turn out 3,600 tons per annum, and pay- ing for everything, this company will have cash capital for the ordinary working of the business of about £15,000 which is considered amply sufficient. There are at least 19 companies engaged in manufacturing horse nails in A.mer,ea, but in Eng- land (or indeed Europe) there are only two companies which make a partially finished nail by machinery,while as to the field open for this company's operations, it is believed that 2,500 tons of horse nails are sold every month through London mer- chants, and the total use in Europe cannot be less than 6,000 tons per month, or 72,000 tons per annum, and this exch-sive of the Colonies. The present total estimated production by tho company, as before mentioned, yill only be 3,600 tons per year, so it must be seen that there is plenty of room for this company doing even &larger business than is now contemplated. The following Contracts have been entered into, viz.:—A Con- tract dated the 11th day of April, 1881, between the Acm6 Horse Shoe Nail Company, Limited, of the one part, and ERNEST ROBERT PRILEPorrs as Trustee for the United Horse Shoe Nail Company, Limited, of the other part, and a contract dated the 11th of April, 1881, made between the European Globe Nail Coy. of the first part, WILLIAM HENRY REYNOLDS of the second part, and the said ERNEST ROBERT PHILLPOTTS of the third part. As this Company is a going concern, it is, of course, Obvious that there are other contracts with the Company, as to Carrying on the business of the Company, the particulars of which is not considered necessary to set out. LOUI8n• A BIRTHDAY CaTIGHATiILATION. Congratulations in plenty. Some true, some false, I dare say, 0 beautiful sweet-and-twenty, Will be wafted to you to-day. • Some will be borne in the covers Of letters with dainty scent; And some in the vows of lovers With stammering blandishment. Some from the lips of maiden Jealous and nice and untrue; And some from lips that are laden Merely with compliment due. But of wishes from aged or youthful. Be they pleasant, or many, or few, Mine at the least shall be truthful, 0 loveable lovely Lou. 'And I will not recount the graces Of tress, or bosom, or arm. Nor dwell in words on your face's Lovelight and wonder and charm. So with your well-wishes in plenty. t Take mine in poetical feet, For certain as you are twenty • So certainly you are sweet. F. THE WEB OE LIFE. My life, which was so straight and plain, Has now become a tangled skein. Yet Clod still holds the thread; Weave as I may, Ills hand doth guide The shuttle's course, however wide The chain in woof be wed. One weary night, when years went by, I plied my loom with tear and sigh. In grief unnamed, untold; But when at last the morning's light Broke on my vision, pure and bright, , There gleamed a cloth of gold. And now I never lose my trust, Weave as I may—and weave I must— That God cloth hold the thread; He guides my shuttle on its way, He makes complete my task each day; What more, then, can be said ? ?tins. SLOOXFIELD MOORE.

No man can' be wise on an empty stomach. A San Francisco editor says that when he thinks of Ire- land's woes his heart goes "Pity Pat." Waiter (bawling to the cook): "One roast lamb and, one potato.' _ Old Gentleman: "No, -no Not so 'much lamb, and more potatoes." Morel hearts pine away in secret anguish for the want of kindness from those who shouid Iv their coraforteii than for any other calamity in life.—Young., r A Detroit saloonistheattda half-dellai red hot and put it 1 on his bar to see who would slyly pocket it. Over twenty men concluded that it didn't belong to them. "Sally," said a young man to a damsel who had red hair, "keep away from me, or you will set me on fire." "No danger of that," was the answer, "you are too green to

burn." It would 1,2 quite easy, says the Somerville Journal, to pay the national debt by imposing a tax on beauty. There isn't a woman in the country who would not demand to be assessed. A doctor went out for a day's hunting, and, on coming home, complained that he hasn't killed anything. "That's beeause you didn't attend to your legitimate business,"

said his wife. A Dutchman found his way into one of our local tonsorial rooms the other day, and upon being asked how often he shaved, replied " bree times a week, every day but Soon- day: den I shaves every day." Somebody quotes: When a man begins to go downhill he finds everything greased for the occasion, says a philo- sopher, aria the Pkiladelphia relV3 thinks he might have added that when he tries to climb up he finds everything greased for the occasion, too. "Why should a red cow give white milk?" was the sub- ject for discussion in a suburban agricultural club. After an hour's debate the secretary of the meeting was instructed to milk the cow and brisg in a decision according to the merits of the milk. It was blue. When a man dies suddenly, "without the aid of a phy- sician," as an Irishman once said, the coroner must be called in. But if the man dies regularly, after being treated by the doctor, everybody knows why he died, and then the coroner's inquest is not necessary. When you go to Kolozvar, Hungary, tell the newsboy to give you a copy of the Ossskaoonlitto Irodalonzotrlenelnzi Lapak, which everybody calls for when they are in a hurry to see the news. It is a Magyar paper, and it will Magyar jaws ache to pronounce it. A furniture dealer, says the Detroit Free Press, seized upon a woman's baby for a debt of 3 dollars, but after keep- ing it two days he was glad to give his debtor 5 dollars to relieve him of his charge. it baby who can't make life miserable for two or three persons will die very young. GREAT MEN AND THEIR ANTUCEDEtrrs.---If all bio- logical science, enforcing all popular belief, convinces you that by no possibility will an Aristotle come from a father and mother with facial angles of fifty degrees, and that out of a tribe of cannibals, whose chorus in preparation for a feast of human Mesh is a kind of rhythmical roaring, there is not the remotest chance of a Beethoven arising, then you must admit that the genesis of the great man depends on the long series of complex influences which has produced the race in which he appears, and the social state into which that race has slowly grown. If it be a fact that the great man may modify his nation in its structure and actions, it is also a fact that there must have been those antecedent modifications constituting national progress before he could be evolved. Before he can re-make his society, his society must make him Herbert Spencer. MILL—The other morning, when a milk-dealer delivered the usual quantity of so-called to a new customer up town, ' he was met with the accusation, "I found the milk you left yesterday composed of about half water." The dealer muttered an apology of some sort, and hurried away. Next - morning the customer looked very serious, and said, "I found the milk you left yesterday had a great deal of chalk in it." The dealer tried to look astonished, and went away saying he would see about it. Next morning his customer met him with, "I found the milk you left yesterday largely composed of some earthy matter?' "See here," said the dealer, as he squared off, "what sort of a family are you? I've given you three kinds of milk in as many days, and yet you are no nearer being satisfied than at first. I'veMily got one more kind, and if you find fault with that you'll have to get a new milkman."— Wall-street News. TEE LATE Bear. or Carrustass was in some respects a remarkable man. He had a strong liking for mechanics, and in his younger days worked for some time in large en- gineering works in Manchester. He used to tell with some pride that, although he then lived a mile and a half from town, he always walked to his work ready to begin at six o'clock, summer and winter, and was never a day late. He was patentee of several inventions, including an improlTe- meat on the tape-loom, for which he received five hundred pounds ; but he always said, had he been a business man, he should have made a fortune by it, as it has been so gene- rally adopted, and such an immense saving obtained by ita use. Among his other inventions were a gravitating com- pass; a road locomotive, with carriage (in which he, along with the countess, travelled on one occasion from Inverness to Barrogill Castle at the rate of some sixteen miles an hour on the level road, creating quite a sensation) ; a machine for washing railway carriages, Sic. He was the first in the north of Scotland to use the steam plough, by which he reclaimed a large portion of land; and the plough is still sent to various parts of the estate, and the hill ground ploughed free of charge to the tenants.— World. OPTICAL ILLUSION.—When standing by a lake side in the moonlight, you see stretching over the rippled surface to wards the moon a bar of lighte which, as shown by its nearer part, consists of flashes from the sides of separate wavelets. You walk, and the bar of light seems to go with you. There are, even amongst the educated classes, many who suppose this bar of light has an objective existence, and who believe that it really moves as the observer moves —occasionally, indeed, as I can testify, expressing surprise at the fact. But, apart from the observer, there exists no such bar of light; nor when the observer moves is there any movement of this line of glittering wavelets. All over _the4ark- part of-the-surface the undulations are just is bright with moonlight as those he sees; but the light r - fleeted from them does not reach his eyes. Thus, thou there seems to be a lighting of Borne wavelets and not f the rest, and though, as the observer moves, other wavele s seem to become lighted that were not lighted, before, y t both these are utterly false seemings. The simple fa^t s that his position in relation to certain wavelets brings in view their, reflections of the moon's light, while it ke out of view the like reflections of all other wavelets.—Her- bert Spencer.

ea Edwards will contribute papers on the Imperial Family of Russia to early numbers of Harper's Magazine. - Dr. Crevaux is repeirted to have arrived at Trinidad. He ascended the Rio Magdalena as far as Neyva, crossed the Andes to the Croyaleeza, -a head-stream of the Orinoco, followed the the latter to its month. ,The Rev. A. C. Smith, Rector of Yateebur is preparing a coloured "Map of a Hundred Square Miles around Ave. bury," with a key to the British and Roman remains occur- ring there, forming a "Guide to the British and Roman antiquities at North Wilts." The last fragment of the wooden shed which for many yearn disfigured the noble facade of the British Museum has been removed; two Easter Island sculptures, the rudest statues in the world, are all that remain behind the colon- nade, with the architectural effect of which their presence does not interfere. In accordance with one of the last wishes expressed by Thomas Carlyle, a tree has been planted at Eaddington on the site of the house in which John Knox was born, and within view of the churchyard where Mrs. Carlyle lies buried. The expense, including that of an enclosure and a suitable inecription;will be defrayecrby a aiece of Carlyle.— Academe/. It is rumoured that the Greek Government contemplate a continuation of the German excavations at Olympia, which have now ceased. The late Minister, M. Tricoupis, after having touched upon the German work in very high terms, proposed that the enterprise should be continued on a reduced scale for a term of thirty years, and asked the Government to allow a yearly grant for this purpose. "The South Yensington Museum," Part XIV. (London, Sampson Low and Co.) contains drawing Of chair (Venetian —seventeenth century), English cup and cover (silver— Hall mark 1669), a copper gilt pyx -eputed German work, about middle of fifteenth century)o ' cross cat from a single piece of crystal (probably Italian), shell cup and cover (probably German—seventeenth century), and four other plates. Messrs. Neill and Son, of Haddington, announce that they have acquired, and will shortly publish, certain plates by I and after Turner, which have been hitherto unpublished or issued only in very limited edition. They include mezzo- tints and line engravings by lint,* and others, and—what would appear to be a more interesting plate—a full-length portrait of Turner in his studio, drawn and etched by the artist himself. As some doubt seems to exist on the point, it may 65 worth while to explain that the Revised Version of the New Testament is not only the joint property of the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge but that the editions of the ver- sion issued by the two eniversity Presses are identical in very respect except in regard to the word "Oxford" or "Cambridge" on the title pages. The type, form, binding, and price are the same.—Atheneeum. The library which belonged to the late Algernon Holt White, but was in fact collected by Thomas Holt White, edi- tor of Milton's " Areopagitica," was sold by Messrs. Sotheby, Wilk4eson, and Hodge, on Tuesday and Wednesday. A copy of Shakapeare (the second folio) sold for £43; the edition of the Plays, with notes by Johnson and Steevens, in 15 vols., on large paper, for £4O; the first collected edition. of Shakespeare's Poems for £37; and the 1655 edition of his "Rape ' of Lucrece" for £l2 ss. In the same sale, Shelton's transla- tion of" Don Quixote," wanting frontispieces, brought £3; Danyel'e " Poetical Essays" and "Delia," £27 103. ; Mo- rant's " Eesex," two vols., £l6 55.; and Hakluyt's "Voy- ages," £l6 ss. GASES SINGING TEEIR OWN DENSITIES.—The accurate weighing of gases for the determination of their specific gravities is a delicate and difficult operation, in spite of all the devices that have been invented. A new and curious one has lately been proposed by Herr Goldschmidt, whcetx- torts from the gas a vocal declaration of its own density by simply filling a tube, first with air, -and then with the gas or vapour to be tested, striking the tube when thus filled, and recording the note emitted. Having obtained this record, and stated the number of vibrations of the air by the number of the gas, and the square of this quotient expresses the specific gravity of the gas, that of air being unity. I may add that the number of vibrators due to all the notes of the diatonic and chromatic scales has already been determined and tabulated ; for the determination of the intermediate tones, I presume that a siren, or instru- ment producing the same tone as the gas by successive im- pulses that can be counted, would be required. Recent excavations at Combs Hill, Kingston-on Thames, have yielded numerous relics of the early British period. The factilia include small cup-like vessels of coarse dark clay, hand made, and not turned on a wheel, whorls, a mould, and a slab or tile pierced with rough holes ; the metal re- mains consist of pieces of unwrought bronze, spear heads, and colts. In one of the food vessels some grains of wheat still remain. Extensive diggings in the new red sandstone, on the site of an ancient burial-place at Stapenhill, near Bur- ton, are revealing seine interesting phases of archaic British sculpture. Among the finds are urns of ornamental design with burnt human bones; a female skeleton with left arm crossed on the breast, and highly ornamental arm by the side and iron buckle; glass and amber beads with a fasten- ing for a necklace, hand made drinking cups, an urn con- taining a small fibula and fictile beads, another with teeth, part of a skull, a buckle, beads, and a Roman coin of the " Urbs Rome" type pierced, to be worn as a personal orna- ment • and a third urn with burnt bones and highly orna- mented ivory beads. The skeletons lie in various positions, and are associated with several types of weapons. The most important feature is the presence of pieces of flints in close proximity to some of the bones. ELECTRICITY AND THE ANNOUNCEMENT OF FIRE.—An interesting paper on this subject was recently read by M. Bartelousbeforothe scientific section of the Synclical Union of Brussels. He divided the systems for electrical announce- ment of fire into five groups.:—l. Those in which alarm of fire can only be given by addressing a police or fire brigade station, electricity being merely used between such stations (Paris is an example). 2. Those in which the telegraph system is extended to electric alarms, either requiring special management or acting automatically; and in the latter case either completely free to the public or only to be set in action by certain persons (these are general in Ger- many ; they are also found in England and Holland). 3. Those in which an alarm of fire can be given without leav- ing the house (e.g., New York). 4. Local arrangements, in which by means of thermometer alarms individuals are in- formed of the beginnings of fire in a building. 5. Systems In which electricity are not only used to transmit alarms of fire, but to aid the despatch of succour (e.g. in San Fran- cisco the harness is dropped on the horses, the gate bolts are drawn, the gates opened, &c., by electrical agency, and in 50 seconds the fire-engine Is ready to start). M. Bartelous stated, on the evidence of statistics, that with the most per- fected systems serious fires were reduced to 4 per cent.; with systems of telegraph linese but without alarms, they still reached 17 per cent.; while without telegraph office they reached 27 per cant. He recommended that the tele- graph offices now open be authorised to transmit alarms of fire free of cost to the sender, and that this use of the offices be indicated by placards. Pima AIR IN THE BEDROOM.—HOW much air can be safely admitted into a sleeping or living room is a common question. Rather, it should be considered, how rapidly air can be admitted without injury or risk, and at how low a temperature. We cannot have too much fresh air so long as we are warm enough and are not exposed to draughts. What is a draught? It is a swift current of air at a temperature lower than the body, which robs either the whole body or an exposed part of its heat so rapidly as to disturb the equilibrium of our circulation and give us cold. Young and healthy persons can habituate themselves to sleeping in even a strong draught, as from an open window, if they cover themselves in cold weather with an abundance of bed- clothes. But those who have been long accustomed to being sheltered from the outer air by sleeping in warmed and nearly or quite ehutup rooms are too susceptible to cold to bear a direct draught of cold air. Persons over seventy years of age,moreover,withlower vitality than in their youth, will not bear a lower temperature even in the air they breathe. Like hothouse plants, they may .be killed by a winter night's chill, and must be protected by warmth at all times. As a ruleTwi may say. that, except for the most robust, the air which enters at night into a sleeping chamber should in cold weather be admitted gradually, only by *racks or moderate openings, or should have its force broken by some interposed obstacle, as a curtain, dm., to avert its blowing immediately on a sleeper in his bed. The ancient fashion, however, of having bed curtains which excluded almost all the air, has rightly become almost obsolete. No wonder that people dream horrid dreams, and wake in the morning wearied rather than refreshed, when they sleep in rooms sealed up tightly on every side, breathing over and over again their own breaths, which grow more poisonous with every hour of the night. IRON FLOATING ON IRON.—For more than a century the ironfoundels have succeeded in puzzling the philosophers by showing them an experiment quite familiar in the foundry, but questioned and even denied in the lecture-room and learned society. This experiment is the throwing of a lump of cold iron into a pot of melted iron. The solid iron, in- stead of sinking, as it should if it behaved according to laboratory determinations of its specific gravity, contradicts them flatly by rising to the surface and floating upon the melted metal of lower specific gravity than itself. An ac- count of the controversies and attempts at explanation that have been connected with this experiment would fill a whole number of this magazine, but one has been lately offered' which really seems to solve the mystery. Professor Chandler Roberts and Mr. Wrightson have invented an instrument for measuring the specific gravity of heated metals, and find that, although cold iron, or completely solidified iron, is un- questionably more dense than melted iron, it becomes ab- normally expanded just before melting, or the temperature at which it assumes that plastic condition which rendersj welding possible; and thus it floats when it reaches this i temperature. Having repeated the popular foundry experi- ment, lam prepared to support this theory. I noticed that in every case the metal sank, then presently it rose and floated, but I attributed the sinking to the force of projec- tion. Now the idea is suggested, I remember that the up- rising was slower than it should have been as a mere result of immediate buoyancy, and that the time which elapsed was sufficient for the heating of the lump to the temperature named by Messrs. Roberts and Wrightson. Besides this, there is a peculiar porosity in iron at this temperature—so great, that under the hammer it appears like a sponge; and I suspect that a frothing then occurs due to the loosening el some of the gases which are occluded or solidified within the cooler metal. If this is the case, the increase of +Adz+ or porosity due to this increase of gas explains the special diminution of specific gravity at this temperature. Graham extracted hydrogen and other gases that were occluded or solidified within various samples of iron by merely heat- ing them and then pumping out the gases from the pores which their evolution had created.—Gentleman's Magazine.

div.head: A_"PRIL .21S, 4881 . 'ES. MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: A_"PRIL .21S, 4881 . 'ES. MISCELLANEOUS.

Mr. Thomas Isherwood, a Liberal, has been elected as the first mayor of the new municipal borough of Heywood. old•man named William Inglesert, living at Middle- ton, died while reading the account of Lord Beaconsfield's

A fall of stone, 25 yards long, took place at New Seaham Colliery on Wednesday, imprisoning several miners. Men are erigaged clearing away the fall, but it was 'not expected to reach those entombed till morning. Sounds have been heard proceeding from behind the fall. Mr. Francis Hartley, a retired solicitor, who with his family had taken an active part in m2Bt philanthropic move- ments in Exeter, was found dead on Monday morning, and at the inquest it -was shown he had expired from heart disease. A correspondent calls attention to the collapse of the electric light on ;London Bridge, and says it was no wonder that the illumination failed. The electric cable, it seems. was mistaken for a hawser by passing barges, who used it to make fast their .craft. Another portion of the ruins of the tower of the beautiful old church of St. John's Chester, fell on Tuesday, and there is little doubt that the rest of the tower will come down during the first gale of wind, bringing the magnificent peal of eight bells with it. On Monday night a boy, six years of age, named James Campbell, died at Annan from the effects of eating hemlock roots in mistake for earth nuts. Three companions, three years older, who had bean wish him along the river side, were also seriously ill, but recovered under medical treat- ment.

At the Manchester Quarter Sessions, the Recorder, ad- dressing the Grand Jury, s aid he was sorry not to be able to congratulate them on any diminution of crime in the city. Though none of the offences was of a particularly serious nature, the number of prisoners for trial was unusually large. At Tuesday's sitting of the Grand Lodge of English Good Templars' at Southampton, it was reported that the juvenile branch of the order numbers 51,064 persons. A builiing and land hare been purchased at Sunbury for the purposes of the Templar Orphanage, with accommodation for sixty children. Mr. Briggs, member for Blackburn, speaking at the open- ing of a Liberal Club, on Saturday, asked which was true courage—to confess that we were wrong or to trample our foe to death. The hon. member accused Sir Owen Lanyon of hoodwinking Her Majesty's late Government, and said that incapable representatives should be recalled. The House of Lords is endeavouring to give a singular privilege to the much-abused British soldier. He is to have the right to be flogged if he wishes. That is the short effect of Lord Denman's bill. When a soldier appears before a court-martial, and is convicted and sentenced to imprison- ment, he may be put to his election. He may call on his judges to order a summary lashing, but the limit of the punishment is fixed at 25 strokes. Lord Cloneurry, writing in reply to a memorial from his tenants requesting reductions of rent, says he cannot grant any reduction, but that any tenant, excepting such as hold leases and occupy lands adjoining Glenstaff, who are de- sirous of purchasing the fee simple of their farms, can have the same at his hands by paying 24 years' purchase on the existing rental. If not, the alternative is that he will place the lands in the hands of his solicitor.

Mr. BRIGHT ON PROTECrION.—Mr. Bright, writing to gentleman in Bradford on the subject of protection as a remedy for depression in the worsted trade, says: You have had great prosperity wil h the present tariffs, and the sup- position that your case will be improved by refusing to buy what you want from foreigners seems to me an idea worthy only the inmates of a lunatic agyium. Great expansion is followed by depression, to be Li. .wed, I believe, by a return to a fair measure of prosperity. An exhibition of a novel caaracter is to be held in the Agricultural Hall, Islingt„d, in August next. It will com- prise all temperance and non-alcoholic drinks, the mackinery for their preparatien, and the various modes of packing them, as well as machinery for cork cutting, bottle cleaning, and kindred industries, and there will also be shown a quan- tity of artistic tea and coffee services in silver and china, and as being peculiarly appropriate to the season, ice- making machines and appliances for refrigeration. The profits accruing are to be devoted to the benefit of a well- known temperance institution. A painful scene occurred on Wednesday at the Bir- mingham Quarter Sessions. Mary Lee, who had been re- peatedly convicted in Glasgow, Liverpool, and Birming- ham, and who, it was stated, was driven into a life of crime by the illtreatment of her husband, was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. The prisoner immediately fainted in the dock, and a young woman who was sent to gaol for three months for the same offence piteously appealed to the assistant-recorder to be allowed to lighten her companion's punishment by bearing part of the sentence herself. THE NATIONAL LIBERAL LEAGUE.—At a meeting 011 Wednesday, in London, of the council of the National Liberal League, it was unanimously decided that the league should at once resume active operations; and a report of the special committee Was adopted and ordered to Le issued. This report appeals for increased support, in order that the league may vigorously prosecute its work both in London as its centre, and in the home, sourthern, and eastern counties of England more especially, and advocate a reform of the land laws, of local and imperial taxation, of Parliamentary representation, and of the laws relating to bribery. FUNERAL OF THE REV. W. M. PUNSLION.—The funeral of the Rev. W. Morley Punshon, LLD.' ' the eminent Wes- leyan minister, took place at Norwood Cemetery, on Tues- day. A preparatory service was held in Brixton-hill Chapel, at one o'clock, when the Rev. Ebenezer Jenkins, President of the Conference, addressed a crowded congregation. At a iicarter-past two o'clock the funeral cortege, which included seventeen carriages, proceeded to the cemetery. Present at the grave were the Revs. E. Jenkins and Marmaduke C. Osborne, the Lady Mayoress, Dean Stanley, dec. The ser- vice at the grave was read by the President of the Confer- ence. Deceased leaves a widow and two children. A labourer, who was further described as a local preacher, was sent to gaol for three months by the Bootle magistrates upon a charge of theft. The police gave the man a ter- rible character for profligacy; and a negress, who was for- merly a stewardess, declared that after the fellow had lived with her under promise of marriage he caused her to be convicted of stealing his property. It was stated that the prisoner preached from the Salvation Army platform. He pleaded to the local bench that he had been a teetotaller for fifteen years; but the court very properly declined to regard this solitary virtue as a sufficient set-off against the black hypocrisy which was alleged against him. A national conference of miners was opened at Birming- ham, on Wednesday, to consider the question of sliding scales of wages; Mr. B. Pickard, vice-president of the Miners' National Union, presiding. 'Delegates representing 195,000 workmen in England and Scotland attended. Re- ports were submitted showing that sliding scales were estab- lished in Durham, Northumberland, Cleveland, West York- shire, Cumberland, South Staffordshire, and other places, and that the wages of 150,000 men were regulated in that way. The conference will probably last three days. The election of the forty-eight executive council of the Ancient Order of Foresters took place on Wednesday, at Weymouth. Bro. Wm. Tiley Houndsell was elected High Chief Ranger, and John Moon High Court Treasurer, and the remaining officers were—High Court Secretary, George B. Symonds; Senior Warden, Richard Rashley ; Junior Warden, Frederick J. Stockling ; Senior Beadle, W. Rogers Symonds; and Junior Beadle, Samuel Coysh. This execu- tive council will have the entire management of the Order after the High Court meeting at Northampton in August. The Order now numbers 568,000 members. CREDULITY me Turs BLACK COTINTRY.—At the Dudley police-court, Ellen Lovell, of Kate's Hill, was charged with. obtaining .money by pretending to tell fortunes. Celia Peters, married woman, said the defendant learned from the neighbours that she was in trouble, and then came to her and told her that she was bewitched by a black woman. For 9s. she would take the witching off her and clear the house of witchcraft. The complainant was to poor to find 28., but she gave up part of her grocery and some money, whereupon the gipsy, Lovell, gave her a bottle of stuff to burn at mid- night, using the left hand only. Witness was so weak and ill through trouble that she really believed she was bewitched. —The bench sentenced Lovell to a month's imprisonment, with hard laboar, and told Peters she was a weak, silly woman to believe such rubbish. Mr. Coddiagton, M.P., and Major-General Feilden, M.P., spoke at the opening of a Church bazaar at Blackburn, on Wednesday. Mr.Coddington said that in the last decade Church scholars had increased from 800,000 to 1,500,000; voluntary grants from £343,000 to £587,000; and the total amount from £1,000,000 to £2,500,000. Seven thousand pounds had been raised by bazaars for Church objects in twelve months in Blackburn, and one should be promoted for building another church. Major-General Feilden said that without religious instruction education could not be advantageous. He declared that Mr. Bracllatigh had no more right to take his seat in the House of Commons this year than he had last, and his imgression was that there would be violent opposition to his doing so. He hoped Con- servative members would speak out, though a good many were afraid to do so. The Easter Monday Volunteer Review, held at Brighton, proved a great success. Some 25,000 troops were engaged, and the weather was fine, though as the day advanced a high wind raised clouds of dust, and rendered matters anything but pleasant for spectators. Prince Edward of Saxe- Weimar was in command of the forces; the Duke of Con- naught had charge of one division, and the Commander-in- Chief, attended by a brilliant staff, witnessed the march past after the field operations. These consisted in an attack by some 20,000 men under General Higginson upon a posi- tion taken up by General Earle, with 5,000 men, who were supposed to have taken up a very strong position after land- ing. Vast crowds Sf people attended the review. There were some casualties, but nothing of a serious nature is

reported. A GOOD FRIDAY ADVENrunE.—At Llanfairfechan, a Liverpool excursionist, who had gone for a walk upon the Lavan sands, had a very narrow escape. He was suddenly surrounded with the fog, and although a native of the place, he found himself unable to reach dry land. Fortu- nately be got out of reach of the full height of the incom- ing tide, and, having been missed, men on horseback were sent out on the sands, but without success. The church bell was then rung continuously, and, guided by its sound, the missing one, who for two hours had been standing waist high in the water, was at last enabled to reach the beitch, and emerged out of the fog just when a large relief party was about to set out. The mist was stated to be one of the densest experienced for many years on this portion of the coast, and objects were with difficulty discerned at five yards distant.

EASTER 'VEST id ES.
RUNCORN.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with the Run- c,)tn Parish Church was held in'the chancel, on Monday. The Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were- also present Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., Mr. Wm. Whittaker, , Mr. Meadowcroft, Mr. Peter Briscoe, and Mr. Wm. Sutton (clerk). The churchwardens' accounts were laid before the meeting, and showed that the receipts from pew. and other sources amounted to £lBB 9s. Id. The expenditure had been £l5B Ds. Id., leaving a balance in favour of the parishioners of £29 13s. 10d.—Mr. Briscoe propose 1, and Mr. Whittaker seconded a motion, which was agreA to, in ' favour of the passing of the accounts.—Mr. Brumli it was re-appointed vicar's warden.—Mr. Briscoe proposed, and Mr. Whittaker seconded a motion that Mr. Crosby be re- elected parishioners' warden which was passed unanimously. —Mr. Whittaker and Mr. warden, were re-elected sidesmen. —On the proposition of Mr. Briscoe, seconded by Mr. Meadowcroft, Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. Whittaker were chosen as representatives of the church at the Ruridecanal and Diocesan conferences.—The next business was the con- sideration of an application from Mr. Wm. Houghton, the apparitor of the church, for an increase of salary.—Mr. Brundrit referred to the custom of the apparitor going round athongst the parishioners for contributions at Christmas time, Ind said that the sum he now raised in this manner was con- eiderably below what he had obtained in former years. He, therefore, considered that the present salary was net suf- Scient.—ln reply to Mr. Brundrit, Mr. Houghton said the amount he received from seatholdere last Christmas, WEI about £4 less than in previous years.—lt was resolved on the motion of Mr. Whittaker, secorided by Mr. Meadowcroft, that in future the apparitor should be paid £l2 per annum, and his wife £3 each twelvemonths for cleaning the church. —Mr. Briscoe proposed a vote of thanks to the choirmaster and choir for their services, And spoke of the very creditable manner in which the musical part of the services had been rendered during the past year. He considered that they *tight tq. recognise the services of the choir. In some churches &special collection was made in order to defray the cost of giving the choir a summer out.—Mr. Whittaker had pleasure in seconding the motion, and he expressed a hope that they would be able to give the choir a trip be- fore long.—The Parish Clerk /submitted a Statement showing that dtuddthe year the total amount subscribed at the various collections had been £3ll 178. Id. This eum showed a slight falling off, as compared with the previous year.—A vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceedings. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH. The annual Easter vestry meethsg in connection with the Parish Chinch was held in the vestry on Tuesday. There were about a dozen persons present, and the rector, the Rev. W. Quekett, presided. Mr. DOOLEY (churchwarden) said the income for the year had been £386 Bs. el., and they had a balance in hand of £5 58. 4d., but there was £25 owing to the choir, which would leave them about £2O behind. Last year they were about £39 in debt, so that their position was considerably improved. Alderman WEBSTER moved, and Mr. WOODS seconded that the accotaits be passed, and the proposition was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN re-appointed Mr. W. Dooley as his warden, and on the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Mr. Wooris, Mr. S. Davies was appointed the people's warden. Mr. DOOLEY moved that a voluntary church rate of 3d. in the pound be laid. The rate had produced £3l 17s. sd. for the last year. He added, in answer to Alderman Web- ster, that the previous year it realised £33 2s. Id., but they paid £5 9s. 9d. for collecting, whilst this year they had only paid £1 12s. Mr. DAVIES secouded the motion, which was carried. On the motion of Mr. DOOLEY, seconded by Mr. DIMES, Alderman Webster and Mr. Buckton were appointed dele- gates to represent the church at the conference which would be probably held at Liverpool in the summer. Messrs. Nicholson and White were re-appointed vestry clerks. Mr. BIICKTON asked whether any steps bad been taken to obtain possession of the land at Woolston which the poor ought to have. The CHAIRMAN Said that acting under the advice of of Messrs. Nicholson and White he had taken no action is the matter. Mr. Bucirrow said it was not the rector or incumbent that had to do with it. It was in the hands of the church- wardens and the overseers.
The Cnainitax said nothing had bees done since the last meeting. Alderman WEBSTER said he thought it was the church- wardens and overseers of Padgate who had to do with the matter.

Mr. WOODS: You would not advise them to go to law in this matter, Mr. Buckton ? Mr. BITETON : I would advise them to get it. The matter should not have beets allowed to run on as it had been. He did not think the parties who had the land took it dis- honestly, but by mistake in the marking out 'of the boundary, and the moment the error was pointed out to them they would at once rectify it, and willingly restore it to the poor. Mr. WFIITH said the whole thing hsd been gone into, and the party who was said to have the land had paid for it by measurement, and he wanted to know how he was to be idemniqed if he gave it up. Some further conversation took place, after which the CHAIRMAN said Mr. Buckton might be satisfied that they would do the best they could in the matter. The proceedings then terminated.

ST. JAMES'S CHURCH, LATCHFORD. The annual Easter vestry meeting in connection with St. James's Church, Latchford, was held in the vestry at noon on Monday. The Re'. F. Slater, vicar, presided. There were about 20 persons present. Mr. ASHTON, the senior warden, was unable to produce the vouchers for several accounts, and as it was impossible that the meeting could then pass the accounts, Mr. l'esLott suggested that Mr. Ashton prepare a balance sheet, and nail it to the church door nest Sunday. Mr. Dior Errs: Will it be legal on the part of this meeting to do so? A PeuISHIMErt: I should think not.

Mr. DICKENS: You will have to adjourn the meeting. Mr. T. Asncnorr thought if Mr. Ashton was allowed a few hours in which to put the accounts straight, it would be found all right. He had left it to someone else, and some- one else had not done it. Mr. TAYLOR: I don't think there is any mistake at all. The CHAIRMAN: I think Mr. Ashton has been cheating himself. He has put down more than he really has received. A parishioner suggested that the other business be pro- ceeded with. Mr. ASHCROFT said they could not get through the busi- ness without passing the accounts. They were bound to see the cheques were right before they proceeded to any other business. (Hear, hear.) Mr.TaYLOrt asked if the meeting could be adjourned until seven o'clock that night? The CHAIRMAN said he would be unable to be present. He thought the proper course was to choose their wardens, and then those that were interested could have the accounts put before them that night, or at any other convenient tune. Mr. DICKENS maintained in all fairness that that could not be done. He should retire from the meeting, and he knew several others would do the same, if any business was proceeded with prior to the passing of the accounts. It was an illegal act to do so. The CHAIRMAN disputed Mr. Dickens' objection and did not see any reason why they should adjourn the election of wardens from the present moment. He should be glad to have the feeling of the meeting on the matter. Mr. DICKENS said he had taken opinion on the matter, and though it was not legal opinion it was practical opinion that no business could be transacted until the accounts were passed. Mr. AsticnOrr did not see any difficulty in the accounts, and they could adjourn the meeting to suit Mr. Slater. They ought to be in a position to pass the accounts without any demur. I A PAR/SHIONER lIONv would it be to pass the accounts as read. Mr. Asncnorr : How can they be passed? That is a stupid idea. The CHAIRMAN : The question is: shall we adjourn the whole business or go on to the eleetion of wardens, and have another meeting afterwards to pass the accounts. Mr. ASHCROFT proposed that the meeting be adjourned to some early hour—any hour the chairman liked to name. Mr. Fey: I beg to propose that we go on to the election of wardens. Mr. ASHCROFT : Are you a parishioner? Mr. FRY Yes. Proof was being given but Mr. ASHCROFT said he would accept his word. Mr. DICKENS seconded Mr. Ashcroft's motion, and the amendmett was seconded by Mr. WORRALL. Frost seconded, the re-election of Mr. T. Ritchie as the parishioners! sidesman, which was also carried unani- mously.—Dr. J..W Watkins asked for a burial or obligatory rate of id. in the viand, which was put to the meeting and carried.—The Chairman, referred at length to the insecure state of the balky and the necessity- of immediate action being taken in the matter. He regretted that the bell could not be used as-its vibration seriously affected both the bell turret and the west wall of the church, and be asked his war- den to read the reports and correspendtnce bearing on the point.—Dr. Watkins said the wardens had been delayed in , taking official steps respecting this very important matter as they were not sworn in until the 17th of June, 1880. After that they obtained reports from Mr. Cornelius Sherlock, of Liverpool, and an estimate for carrying out the proposed alterations from Mr. J. Pennington amounting to 13197, and; ; towards that amount, including promises, ;there would be ' forthcoming about £l2O. When Mr. Pennington submitted his estimate he pointed out that some of the principal beams. were not firm enough to bear the pressure. Mr. C. Sherlock upon this sent in a second report, which recommended dis- pensing with a belfry, dm. That was how the matter stood, and the wardens would not of themselves take any respen- eibility, or spend any money on the work till they got it, and they placed themselves entirely in the hands of the vestry as to what action should be taken.— Mr. Pardey had seen the church, and was quite aware of its leading defects. He felt favourable to Mr. Sherlock'a first report, and would be sorry to see a belfry dispensed with. He knew that the principal pinnacles were straight and sap- ported from the base, therefore he saw no reason why a thoroughly practical man could not place a sort of key arch on which to rest a lighter-constructed belfry. So desirous was he to see a good plan carried out that he would increase Mr. Legh's donation to £5O and his own to £lO. The whole thing, be believed, could be well and effectively donelor about £25O.—A very long discussion ensued, in which Messrs. Comber, McCorquodale, Clarke, Houghton, Pardey, 'Dr. Watkins; Moister, and the Chairman took part.—Ulti-L , mately, Mr. T. Comber said he firmly believed if the structural difficulty could be got over successfully, the money to carry' out the object would be forthcoming. (Hear, hear.) Hel therefore proposed that the opinion of Mr. John Pierpoint, of Warrington be obtained as to the true position of the edifice, and the probable cost of putting it in safe and be- coming condition, and that any further consideration of the matter be adjourned for a fortnight, when another meeting could be held and the question settled.—Mr. G. McCorquo- dale considered that was the most practical way of settling ' a question on which such a difference of opinion existed, and therefore seconded the motion, which was adopted.— The appointment of ruri-decanal representatives was not definitely made, but two will be selected from the follow- ing :—Mr. J. H. Birley, Dr. Watkins, and Mr. J. Devereux. .The Dean School Trttet is in active operation, and an en- couraging statement was submitted :by Dr. Watkins.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman, on -the rnotion,ot- Mr. MoCorquodale, seconded by Mr. Comber, closed the pro- ceedings.

ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The annual meeting of the parishioners connected with this church was held on Monday, the vicar, the Rey. S. Wilkinson, in the chair. There were also present the Rev. E. St. A. Duke (curate) and Messrs. Thomas Sutton,Thomas Jolley, John Pierpoint, John Hough, W. D. Jeans (vestry clerk), and George Bebbington (clerk). Mr. SUTTON gave a statement of the churchwardens' accounts, from which it appeared there had been received from pew rents, £39 15s. od.; fortnightly collections, £55 14s. ; tea party, £49 14s. 7d. ; total, £145 4s. 26. The payments for the year, including 10 guineas paid to Mr. Pierpoiut on account of the plans for the proposed church alterations amounted to £144 2s. 66., leaving a tialanee in hand of £l,2s.SThere were some accounts owing, and then not having the usual collection for the choir left them £36 4s. 7d. to the bad. The accounts were passed, on the motion of Mr. Pena- POINT, seconded by Mr. HOUGH. The Cntanntax thanked Mr. Jolley for his past services as vicar's warden, and said he had pleasure in asking him to serve again. He and Mr. Sutton had been first and foremost in every good work during the past year, and it was especially needful, when they had in contemplation the restoration of the church, that both gentlemen should remain in office. (Hear, hear.) Mr. JOLLEY, in accepting the position, expressed a hope that they would succeed in carrying out the contemplated alterations to the church. It had been their desire to help the Vicar to the best of their ability. (Hear, hear.) Mr. PIERPOINT proposed the re-electiou of Mr. Sutton as people's warden. Mr. 11000 K seconded the motion, which wo carried. Mr. SUTTON, in reply, said he hoped at the end of the year he would be as deserving of their confidence and kind- ness as at the present time. He trusted that during the year they would be able to accomplish what they all desired, and that was to restore the church. It was very necessary that the work should be commenced as soon as possible. It would be better for the vicar, curate, and parishioners, and they would be able to accommodate mere people. (Hear, hear.) Mr. G. Grange, and Mr. Thomas Morris were appointed sidesmen, and Messrs. D. W. Finny, and John Pierpoint were appointed to represent the Church at such conferences of the clergy and lefty of the deanery of Winwick, as may be held during the ensuing year. Votes of thanks to the chairman, vestry clerk, and church- wardens, terminated the meeting.

They could not afford to put their trust in promises.—Mr. Chadwick said he had not the slightest intention of touching the vicar's stipend.—Mr. ' Balmer said that supposing they adopted the original motion-, they could not get any more people. into the edifice at night than were in attendance now, as a.rule. He asked where the people were in a morning who had such a treat anxiety to attend church.—Mr. Treacy, junr., remarked that there was a natural timidity on the part of some people to, occupying pews which belongedto.other people.— Mr. Bahner said there were two sorts of free seats in the church, a number of which were at the hack and others at the front, but neither were occupied.—Mr. Tracey, jun., was quite willing to alter the form of his proposition, but be ,should be glad to know when it could be brought forward to have a decision taken upon it.—Mr. Crabtree said some of the seathoiders did not give up their sittings with a good 'grace, and others had a decided objection to vacating them at all. As soon as the service commenced. 'some seatholders took up their positions at the very entrance to their pews, so that anyone going into them must force their way past. •Mbny stayed away from church because they considered they would be encroaching on some one else's privileges if ' they went, though, at the same timo,. they were Churchmen heart and soul. If the deficiencyin the contributions was ' intended to be made up by an oz.-tension of the offertory : system, the adoption of such a course might result in the Chairman having no supporters. Mr. Treaey, jun., had his ; hearty support In this matter.—Mr. Lord could not say that he had noticed that people had an objection to others going into their seats. A man,however, liked to have the oppor- tunity of sitting down first in his. own house--(langhter)— and probably this feeling extended to pews.—The Chairman 1 could hardly think that the people spoken of as being ' Churchmen heart and soul could really be so, or they would, - find their way to church. (Laughter.)—Mr. Midge said 1 there were pewholders who. would not even make room ' for members of the congregation who had been put oat of their own seats, so that they had no need to deal with the case of strangers. Some he had to tap on the shoulders before they would move, and even when they did so, they gave him a very "downy look." Five voted for Mr. Atherton's amendment; and ten for, and eix against that of Mr. White, that the old systeni should be adhered to. • This amendment was then put as the substaative motion and passed.—The Vicar chose as hl warden *Mr. J. Jones, and W. Hagley.—The three retiring parishioners' sidemen, Messrs.J. Lord, W.Treacy, junr., and CAI, Kennion were re- elected, and Mr. D. H. Lwvvry was also elected as an addi- tional churchwarden.—The lay representalves elected were Messrs. Matthews, and White.—A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman on the motion of Mr. Balmer, seconded by Mr. Imison, arid the proceedings, which were of a very pro- tracted character, terminated.

The annual meeting in connection with Widnes Parish Church, was held iu the school room, on Monday; and was one of more than usual importance. Tbe chair was occupied by the Reve.K Wright-Williams, vicar; and there were also present tha Rev W. H. Duggan, curate ; Messrs. W. Treacy, W. R. Imieon, Lewis Kllcross, We Crabtree, T. Bracegirdle, repairs to roof, £Bl Mr. Jonas Foster, slates, &c., .£6 4a.; Messrs. J. Handley and Co., lead, etc., £3 is. 7d.-The Chairman said the statement of accounts would now be laid upon the table, and be open for the examination of any of the gentlemen preseat.-Mr. Treaey thought it well to state that the ac- counts had all been examined by the auditor in detail, and signed by him.-Mr. James White said he was asked to audit the accounts, and he went through them very care- fully, He found that every collection made in the church wascorrectly placed in the accounts. As to the other side of the account, he did not consider it necessary to examine that quite as carefully, as any omissions under that would; affect the pockets of the churchwardens themselvese (Laughter.)-Tbe accounts were passed, on the motion of Mr, T. Balmer, seconded by Mr. It lidge.-The Chairman said, that, whilst the year had been second to none in the amount of work, it had also been second to none in respect to the way in which the churchwardens and sidesmen had worked. He felt personally grateful to each of the church officers for the manner in which they had discharged their duties.- Mr. Chadwick, in moving a vote of thanks to the retiring officers for their services during the year, remarked upon the regularity of their attendance in comparison with pre- vious years.-The motion having been seconded, Mr. Balmer(' supported it, and said be had never known a year when there had been sounder judgment displayed, or when the relationel between the churchwardens had been more amicable. He had not heard of a single hitch-The question which next , came before the meetieg, was as to what course should be adopted in dealing with the plot of land surrounding the vicarage. Mr. Treacy senior, read minutes of what had been done at various meetings held on the subject by the trustees of the parish. The drat meeting took place at Messrs. Clo3sage's offices, when amongst those present were, Mr. Tim- , mis, and Mr. Brunner. The last named gentleman produced an account from Mr. Samuel White, of Runcorn, amounting fo £63 7s. 64., for five year's rent of the plot of land adjoin- ing the vicarage, and enclosing a note, stating that unless the amount were paid, he weuld take possession of the land and use it for building purposes. The trustees, who had already gone to a considerable amount of trouble and ex- pense in this matter, stated that they did not consider them- selves under any obligation to pay the account; in fact, they ' repudiated their liability as trustees, to do so. They, how- ever, at the same time considered that a moral obligation rested on the churchmen of St. Mary's to do so, inasmuch as a resolution to the effect that it should be discharged had gen passed at the Easter vestry meeting,in 1875. Mr.Timmis observed that if a subscription for the purpose of paying the account were passed, he would be willing to subscribe £lO towards the fund out of his own pocket. (Applause.) The church council, after discussion, had decided that Mr. S. White should be seen, and an effort made to induce him to reduce the amount of his claim. Mr. S. White was met, and, after discussion, he agreed to take £4O in settlement of the account. (Applause.)-A parishioner was of oyinion that they were morally bound to pay the VO, even if they did not take the land for the future.-The Chairman said it appeared to him that their legal position was that the vote in the vestry would give authority to pay the rent, but the wardens were not liaole beyond the funds in hand. If they decided to pay it, it must been moral grounds entirely. It appeared that in the church books there was a resolution about the expenditure at one time of £220 in building a church wall. Now they were in possession of no wall which could account for the expenditure of such a sum of £220 unless it was the one around the vicarage. It was a grievance to find that the bricks around the parsonage had been paid Mr by church money, and yet the lessee now said that they were his, although never paid a penny for them.-Mr. White moved, and Mr. Matthews seconded, a proposition which was carried unanimously to the effect that a subscription should be opened for the purpose of paying Mr. White's bill.-The subject again came up at a later stage of the proceedings.-Mr. Imison read a resolution from the vestry minute book for 1875, to the effect that a certain amount of land adjoining the parsonage should be leased from Mr. White, of Runcorn, at 3d. per yard. Ile also proposed that the resolution should be rescinded.-This was seconded by Mr. Kennion, and passed nem. dis.-Mr. White moved that any future arrangements entered into in regard to the land should be of a yearly character.-Mr. Kilcross seconded the motion, which was agreed to.-Mr. Reunion considered that if Mr. S. White were to build upon the land referred to, it would destroy all the picturesqueness of the vicarage.-The Chairman said that during the last eighteen months he had been subjected to great annoyances. Mr. • Kennion spoke about taking away the picturesqueness of the vicarage. Well, the picturesqueness might be spoken of more or less-(laughter)-perhaps Mr. Kennion referred to the bridge when he used the word. It was suggested that the ground should be taken for one year. But even sup- posing this were done, he had to remind them of the fact that the ground was no use unless the wall was raised. The present lessee claimed the wall; and even supposing that they were to raise it a couple of feet, he might still retain his right to the bricks, and this would be very hard. If they asked Mr. S. White to raise the wall at his expense, he might • decline to do so unless the land was taken, for a period of ten years.-Several reso- lutione on tfte subject were placed before the meeting.- The Chairman, referring to one of the motions, said that if it meant that the next twelvemonths was to be the same as the previous ones-if there were to be the same arid desert- ness-the passing of it would be a mistaken kindness to him. He was very much grieved that there was a twelve- sip Tempe 'rqemnop °um ellqm, eiw--•artp lue.t ,stodout £4O had been paid to Mr. White, he would do the required work, as he was in the trade, and it would not be very expensive for him.-Mr. Balmer very much questioned whether Mr. White would do anything of the kind. As far as be was concerned, he should like to know what the lessee intended to do before they took the land for another twelve months, as at present it was worth nothing at all, owing to the children making it a common playground. • He moved that the matter should be left in the bands of the churchwardens, for the purpose of seeing Mr. White as to whether he would put the fence in proper order, and tbat they be empowered to use their discretion in carrying out whatever plan they might think best.-Mr. Lord seconded the proposition, and, after the other motions had been with- drawn, Mr. Balmer's was passed unanimously.-Mr. Treacy, jun., moved, "That, owing to the Parish Church being most inadequate for Hie accommodation of the Church- people in'St. Mary's parish, it is desirable to make it entirely free am! unappropriated." He considered the plan at pre- sent adopted meant the exclusion of the poor. As Archdeacon Denison said, such people might go to church, but they did not like to intrude. He (the speaker) believed that the adoption of the free and open system afforded the readiest, cheapest, and most effective mode of church extension. He considered that the most important peint he had to urge in favour of his proposal was that the Church of England, being a national church, ought to make herself wholly and entirely the church of the people. To use another quotation from the Venerable Archdeacon, their church must not let it be said at the judgment seat that she had closed the door of the House ot God against the humblest of her children. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman thought the subject more than one of passing interest. He might tell them that his good friend Mr. Treacy, jun., would be the last person in the parish to do anything which would affect him (the speaker) without consulting him. He gave Mr. Treacy, jun., his full consent to the subject being broached, so that he did not cousider the discussion of it an attack upon his interests in the parish. On the contrary, he had sufficient confidence in many of the parishioners to believe that they considered that in bringing the proposal forward they were attacking what was an existing vicious practice. Ventilation of the question would do away with excresences, and blow away some bad thoughts. If the prac- tice at present in existence would not stand discussion, it was not a good one.-Mr. Chadwick seconded the motion, and said he should have been in- clined to use the words absolutely necessary that the seats should be unappopriated if be had been proposing the resolution. To those who wero opposed to such a course being adopted, and who felt contaminated, in a sense, if they
