PADGATE. The annual Easter meeting was held in the vestry of Christ Church, Padgate, on Monday morning; the vicar,. the Rev. W. H. Williams, M.A., in the chair. The accounts presented by the wardens were duly audited, after which Mr. William Royston, of Paddington, was re-elected as the vicar's warden; and Mr. Albert Pennington as the people's warden. Messrs. Royston and Pennington were appointed lay representatives at the ruri-decanal and diocesan con- ferences.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS, WARRINGTON.

On Monday the Easter vestry meeting was held in this church, the Rev. S. Wilkinson in the chair. The accounts having been passed. Mr. John Peers was appointed vicar's warden, and Mr. Woods people's warden. Mr. Bradburn, and Mr. Vernon were appointed sidesmen, and Mr. Rice, and Mr. Gorst were chosen as delegates to represent the church in the diocesan and ruri-deconal conferences.

div.head: ST. ANNE'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. ANNE'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the church on Tuesday, the Rev. J. G. Richards presiding. The -CHAIRMAN complimented the late warden on the manner in which he had performed his duty, but as he would not again stand, he appointed Mr. Gaskell as his warden. Mr. Joseph Bunch was elected people's warden on the motion of Mr. Dagnall, seconded by Mr. Hemment ; and Messrs. Bowes and Sharp were appointed the representatives of the church at the ruri-decanal conference t 3 be held at • Liverpool this year. Mr. Calvert and Mr. Adams were elected sidesmen. Mr. ADAMS said he was sorry there was such a small attendance, because he had left his work specially to come there that day and speak of some few matters connected with the church generally. During the last few years be had not paid that strict attention to church matters that he should have done; but within the last eighteen months or two years he had begun again to take an interest in the affairs of the congregation of St. Anne's Church, and it grieved him very much to see the utter failure of the church in the parish. He should like to know what the number of par- ishioners was. The CLERK: I cannot tell you at the present time. census will probably do so. Mr. ADAMS: We will take it at 7,000 or 8,000. The CHAIRMAN: Oh, no; 4,500. Mr. ADAMS (continuing) said he wondered how much the attendance of parishioners out of that number was. Last Sunday being the greatest festival of the church, he ex- pected that there might have been a good attendance; bat instead he could almost have counted the number of the congregation on the south side of the church on the fingers of two bands, if not on one. There was some reason why the inhabitants of this parish did not attend the church. He should, therefore, like to ask the Vicar if he could give any reason. The CHAIRMAN: I do not see Why such matters should be mentioned at all. Mr. ADAMS: I am speaking in the interest of the church and of the ratepayers. The Cnatumart : Personal matters should not be men- tioned. The reason I think is because most people do not go anywhere; the rest of the people are either Dissenters or they go to other places of worship. That is the fact. Mr. ADAMS said the vicar would now put him down in the same way as he had put some others, that he was a grumbler. But whatever Mr. Richards might say, he had the interest of the church at heart, and only wished its good. They once had a notorious name for being high church. now, that name, they might say, had almost died out, and they were a people who were hardly known in the town. Mr. Richards, when he came to them, objected to a great number of decorations in connec- tion with the church, and, of course, he only drove the majority of the congregation away. lie was now putting up those things again, and on Christmas day he had spoken very strengly The CHAIRMAN: I never spoke against them. If you will introduce these personal matters you had better be stopped. I say you are quite in a mistake; and you are too personal. Mr. ADAMS: This is a vestry meeting, and I say you are quite out of place in stopping me speaking. I say it is my right to speak here. The CHAIRMAN: You take the wrong pig by the tail. Mr. ADAMS said he did not wish to blame anybody • but his opinion was that if increased energy was brought to bear upon the parishioners something might be done to in- crease the attendance at church. Mr. Adams was proceeding to make some personal remarks, when The CLERK said: It is a public meeting, and you should not enter into personal matters any more than is absolutely
The

necessary. Mr. Ams: If I have made any personal reference to hurt anyone, I withdraw the words. The CLERK : Go on. Mr. ADAMS then referred at length to the manner in which drunkenness affected the attendance at church, and said there were greater temptations to drunkenness in that parish than in any other in the town from the fact that there were 18 public-houses, and about the same number of out-door licenses. He suggested that something similar to what was being done in St. Paul's parish should be at- I tempted. The CHAIRMAN said with regard to temperance he

div.head: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

The annual Easter vestry was held on Tuesday, in the v'estryof the church, and afterwards adjourned to the girls' school. The church bell was rung before the meeting, ac- cording to ancient custom. The vicar, Rev. J. Lockwood, presided. There were also present—Messrs. Joseph Stokes and Joseph W. Baguley, Thomas Wright, C. W. Brown, Thomas Acton (Eauley Wood), W. Lambeth (Norton.) 'IT € vicar's and churchwardens' accounts were passed. After paiment of accounts for the past year there is a balance in hand. The vicar re-appointed Mr. Joseph Stokes, of Rock Savage, as his warden. Mr. Joseph W. Baguley, of Stock- ham, was again unaaimously re-elected people's warden. Messrs. Thomas Acton and D. Baguley were appointed sidesmen ; and Messrs. T. Wright and T. Acton the church representatives at the Archidiaconal Chapters. After some discussion it was resolved, "That the 'hey' on the appro- priate seats be the same as last year ;" and "That on the principal festivals of the church processional and reces- sional hymns should be sung."

FARN WORTH. On Monday evening, the annual meeting of the par- ishioners of Farnworth was held in the church. The Rev. G. Holloway, the vicar, occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. g. A. Spooner, curate in charge of St. Ambrose's Church, Appleton; Mr. Brock, Mr. Peter Longton, Cronton Hall ; Mr. Robert Whalley, Bold; Mr. John Knight, Farnworth ; Mr. Taylor, Cuerdley; end Mr. J. W. Davies, Famworth. . . . .

- The churchwardens' accounts, which showed a balance of 16 17s. Oid. in favour of the parishioners, were examined, found correct, and passed. Mr. Whalley was chosen as churchwarden for the parishioners resident in Bold; Mr. Joseph Glover, for Cron- ton ; and Mr. Matthew Taylor, for Cuerdley. Mr. Henry Brunner was chosen by the vicar as his warden. The fol- lowing gentlemen were elected to act as sidesmen:—Major Cross, Messrs. Knight, Roberts, and J. W. Davies. Messrs. Carey, Minton, Williams, Riley, Valentine, Speakman, and Goff were elected as sidemen for the new church of St. Ambrose. Mr. Brock and Mr. Whalley were again chosen to repre- sent the parish at the ruri-decanal and diocesan conference. As at present arranged, collections are made at the church three Sundays in the month towards defraying the churchwardens' expenses, and in aid of the curates' fund. Mr. KNIGHT now expressed his opinion that it would be better to make a collection each Sunday. They would get as much as if one Sunday was missed in the month. The new arrangement would certtinly make some difference in the course of the year, and would put the churchwardens in possession of a sum in hand towards the repair of the fabric of the church, which was greatly needed. Mr. Bnocx : It would not do to leave it to voluntary con- tributions, to be placed in a bowl at the door. Mr. KNIGHT: No. I think we are wrong in having the collecting bags we have at present. I know very often that it is just the tip of the finger, and that nothing is put in the bag. I would suggest that we have plates. Mr. BROCE inquired whether the new arrangement would not have some effect on the attendance at church? The Viciox : I think collections certainly thin the con- gregation. The Rev. S. A. SPOONER remarked that they had collec- tions every Sunday at the Mission Room, where they had bad good congregations since the room was opened. Mr. BRocit considered Mr. Knight's a very good sugges- tion; and would like to see it adopted. The CHAIRMAN also thought it was a valuable suggestio, and was mnch obliged to Mr. Knight for making it. He would rather a suggestion of that sort was made by a par- ishioner than by the clergyman. He believed it was right to make an offering to God a part of religious worship; in fact, he did not think worship was complete without it. A PARISHIONER: Are there no pew rents paid at the church? .

--- Mr.Kmairr. remarked that the church was free, and they ought to look to the parishioners to give at the collections. He thought it ought to be well known that 111 seats were free at Farnworth Church. After a little further discussion regarding the sets occu- pied by the school children, Mr. Knight proposed that there 'be a collection at every service in the church on Sunday, and thet the object for which the collection is made be an-

div.head: ALL SAINTS' CHURCH, THELWALL.
div.p: ALL SAINTS' CHURCH, THELWALL.

The vestry meeting in connection with the above church was held in the schoolroom, The!wall, on Monday, the Rev. T. Pym Williamson in the chair. The churchwardens' ac- counts for the pastyear were audited and confirmed, there being a at-nail balance in hand. The vicar nominated Mr. Norman Taylor as his warden, and Mr. Thomas Cooke was elected the parishioners' warden for the ensuing year.

div.head: TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual vestry meeting at Trinity Church, Run- corn, was held in the vestry on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev. W. Preston, the vicar, and there were also present the Rev. W. Robinson, Mr. fankinson, senior, Mr. liankinson, junior, Mr. John Buckley, Mr. R. Lea, Mr. E. Timmins, Mr. Sefton, Mr. Rogerson, and Mr. Woodwell.— The Chairman said they had made very nice progress during the past 12 months. For the first time during nine years, there was a balance of about £ll to hand over to the incoming warden. The offertories had been somewhat in excess of those of the past two years. Everything ap- peared to be going on very harmoniously; they had made no alterations in the services, nordid they intend to do so.—Mr. John Smith, late vicar's warden, who had held the office for three years, declined to continue in it owing to his health being somewhat indifferent, and his business engagements more numerous than formerly. The vicar chose as his warden Mr. John Buckley.—The latter gentleman nominated as his sidesman, Mr. Hankinson.—On the nomination of Mr. Lea, seconded by Mr. Timmins, Mr. Buck was re-elected people's warden; and that gentleman selected Mr. Rogerson as his sidesman.—Messrs. Fisher and Timmins were also appointed sidesmen and members of the:Church Coundl. Messrs. Fisher and Hankinson were elected delegates to the rut i-decanal and diocesan conferences.—On the motion of Mr. Lea, seconded by Mr. Buckley, a special vote of thanks was given to the choir for their valuable services during the past twelvemonths.—lt was decided, with the object of keep- ing the 'church from getting into debt in future, the offertory should be taken each Sunday evening, and that the offertory on the morning of the first Sunday in the month should be discontinued. •

div.head: FRODSII4M.
div.p: FRODSII4M.

The annual vestry meeting was held by adjournment, in the Boy's School, Overton, on Monday last, when there were present :—Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar (in the chair), Messrs. John Ashton, John Robinson, E. A. Wright, Charles Reynolds, H. Linaker' C. E. Linaker, T. Lewis, T. Davies, J. Pollard, J. Knibb, T. Riley, J. Cunnah, S. Davies, T. Roberts, H. They, R. Andrews, and George Speechley (clerk of works for church restoration).—An important and ex- haustive report was read from the Executive Committee for the Church Restoration, in which they stated that on the recommendation of the architects the dismantling of the church, rebuikking the walls, constructing new windows, arches, dm., restoring pillars, and other work, WAS being canted out by day work, under the direction and supervision of the clerk of the works, and as the stripping of the walls and removing the roofs had been proceeded with from time to time, the adoption of this course had been fully justified, a tanCh worse state of things existing than was anticipated. As would be seen from an inspection of the church, the south aisle roof bad been entirely removed ; and the nave and north aisle roof also. The walls of the south aisle had been partly made good, a new string course and three new widows had been fixed, new priests' doorway and buttresses constructed, the old Norman pillars in the nave cleaned and partly restored, and the arcade of arches on the south side completed, a new Norman arch, two pillars and small pointed arch being substituted for the old wide arch, and the old pier of the south side of the chancel arch; the clerestory windows on this side were almost completed. On the north side of the nave the old lob-aided arch had been removed, and preparations were ; being made for the construction of arches and pillars to cor- respond with the south side. The committee called special attention to the very effective appearance of the old Norman piers after their having been cleaned and restored; the courses of stone in the:shaft came out well, and the richly carved caps were well worthy of inspection, The tower arch had been thrown open, and the stonework of this and of the responds bad been cleaned and restored, and would add , much grandeur to the appearance of the church whea com- pleted. The subscriptions promised, including £5OO from Christ Church, to restore chancel, amounted to £4,491 3e. -104 and £4,341 103. 10d. had been paid to • the treasurer. A font, pulpit, and lectern hid

been promised. The amount required is VAX) The committee expressed their satisfaction of the progress made with the work, under the excellent management/ of , Mr. Speechley.—Mr. H. Linaker mowed that the reporrbe adopted, and that the Executive Committee:be recommended to print the same and forward a copy thereof to each sub- scriber.—Mr. T. Riley seconded the motion, which was carried.—Mr. Wright referred to the :n•oposal made in 1879 for an extension of the burial ground, when Mr. Ashton re.. viewed what had been done in the matter, and after a lengthy discussion a committee was appointed to receive and consider the report of Messrs. Ashton and Garrett, as a formation of a burial board, which was decided upon at a vestry meeting held sth May, 1879. The accounts relating to Harrison's Charity, Overton En- dowed school and Sunday school accounts were produced. The Stockham and Frodsham Charity accounts were not produced. A revised seal of burial fees was produced, but as special notice hadmot been given the matter was deferred. The accounts were audited by Mews. John Pollard and Thomas Riley, and passed, the receipb3 being £95 9s. 6d, and expenditure 178- 17s. 70., leaving a balance in hand of £l6 Ile. lOid. The iron church accounts showed that Dr. Weaver, the late treasurer, had generously given £25 towards the deficit Which hxisted. The atiring church- wardens Messrs. Jelin Ashton- and John: Robinson, were uanimotlsly re-elected, and appointed as lay representatives at the diocesan 'lay conferende. The Wear paid a warm tribute to the Executive Committee for- theft services and expressed his thanks for the ready assistance generally which he had recelved.during the past par. 'I. 4

LYMM PARISH CHDRCH. 1-7-7:11411-1.4 The ananal Ye:9by meeting of the parish of Lymm was held in the vestry of the' church," on Tuesday. Mr. John Parkinson, in the absence of the •Bettor, who was unwell, pecuPied the 'Chair; and there were also present :—Dr. Brabazon'; Messrs. H. A. Schwabe, 'a. 11. Watson, Richard Whitelegg;and Joseph Lawrensonbir. Jonathan Milligan, who has held the office of rector's wattien for six years, was re-appointed, and Mr. Richard iiideelegg was nominated parishioner's warden. The statement of accounts, Submit- ted by Mr. Milligan, showed that the receipts from 'general offertories were £l2l us. 30. At the commencement of the year there was a balance due to the wardens of £l6 18s. 5d., and in order to clear off this deficit Mr. W. Rattensby, of Lymm Hall, gave £9 3s. 5d., and £7 15s. was received from the Rector's offertories. The payments for the year amounted to £l4O 9s. Bid. The accounts were passed unanimously. The accounts of the Prince's Chari- ties were also examined, and the finances were found to be a prosperous state, there being 1.29185. sd. in hand. A vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring warden, Mr. Watson on the motion of Dr. Brabazon, and the meeting terminated.

FRESCO' BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The first meeting of the new Board was held on Mars day forenoon at the Board Room, Whiston Workhouse. There were present the Revs. T. Chambers andJ.Barnaele, Messrs. S. Marsh, Meadows, Buckley, Jackson, Birchall, Rowe, Harrison, Gilbodv, Syder, Renwright, Lowe, Ranson, Fidler, Hall, *Paris, 'Fuson, Birch, Debell, Matthews, Leatherbarrow, Gerrard, Tyrer, Sadler, and Fisher, with.S. H. Hartley, clerk. APPOLITVICENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMEN. _ _

On the motion of Mr. BIRCELLL, seconded by Mr. GER- RARD, Mr. S. Marsh was unanimously re-elected chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Mtasa thanked the Board for the confidence they had reposed in him since he had been chairman of th 3 Board, and hoped that his conduct in the chair the next twelve months would be satisfactory to them and a benefit to the Union Wargo. He was sure they all deplored the depressed state of trade that had prevailed in the Union; but he did not know that the calls had been materially increased. He hoped the coming year would be a prosperous one in every respect, and he hoped the Guardians Would lend him that assistance in the discharge of his duties as they had in previtur years. • _

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL CORN, TRUBSDLY.—Wheat firm, and rod descrip- tions slightly in favour of sellers. Flour remained unchanged. Beans and peas were steady. Maize was stiffer on the spot and near at hand, nEw selling at 5s 4i d per cental. CoRR BUTTER, TTIIIRSDAY. Ordinary: Seconds, 112 e; thirds, 81s; fourths, 58s. Fine mild, 130 s; mad, 115 s, Firkins in the market, t 34.

LIVERPOOL COTTON, TZUBSDAY.—There has been again evi- dent in the spot market a decidedly declining tendency, as the supply offering continues excessive and the demand from the trade very limited. Prices have been irregular throughout, and have been officially reduced 1-16 for the lower grades of American, all East Indian, I-16d to id. for Brazilian, and id. for Egyptian. The reduction in American might well have been extended to the other grades, as business has not been practicable at the official rates. Compared with last week there has been a decline in the official quotations of 1-lid, to id. in American and Brazilian, and id. in Egyptian and East Indian.

MANCHBSTER COTTON, THUESDAY.—The market is generally reported dull and rather drooping, in sympathy with cotton. Yarns certainly are so in almost all branches; but as regards the shirting market things are different. Here, so many of the best-known makes are well under order, aid inquiry for them continues on so large a scale, the market is quite firm, not to say strong or nominally dearer. Of dhootles muoh the same truly be said, and in both departments the business which has been done lately might be easily done again If the rate of pro- duction permitted.

MaNmissTan CORN. TIURSDAY.—T4 cold east 'winds have again prevailed, and vegetation has been retarded. Imports from abroad have been on a liberal scale. This day's market was steady on the whole. English wheat was firm; foreign rather dearer. Flour brought fully previous quotations. Oats brought full prices, especially for lower qualities. Beans declined Id to 2d per eental. Peas were steady. Maize was more plentiful, and cffered at Id p v eental under last week's quotations.

There was quite a scene at the vestry meeting at St. Peter's chinch, Bournemouth, on Tuesday, when the Rev. James Neil, who in not connected in any way with St. Peter's, moved a resolution expressing regret that the vicar and churchwarden had allowed graven images to be placed on the reredos, super-alters to be erected over the communion table, and crosses and candlesticks placed thereon at St. Peter's and St, Swithin's churches, and praying that the vestrylmmediately apply for a faculty for their removal. The resolution, which was not seconded, also provided for preventing Ritualistic clergy preaching in •St. Peter's, and for the abolition of what were considered to be other Ritual- istic practices. Bishop Ryan refused to put the resolution.

Conservatives can soarcely hope that Lord Salisbury as leader would ever inspire the attachment of crowds as Lord tisaconsfield in his later years die- played his art in doing. This is no glamour in the eyes of English Working men as regards the character of Lord Salisbury. He has never inihia life initiated any measure' 'or the bettering or the political and social coalition of the nation's toiling millions. These things oonsidered, we do not believe that the Tory party can be so formidable an enemy to th,li'Llberal party under the leadership of Lord Salishursz itB it has been at times under the Earl of Beaconsfield. is supremacy in the Tory party would Very dikely.be a sharper rod for his followers than for their adversaries. It would, besides, Barely accentrate the alreadffno- nounced opposition of the Earl .of Derby- to Tory interests. At the same time, it is 'just as apparent that the 'nautili 'of, Loyd 'Cairns, the Duke of ,mond, slid, Sir StaffordNorthoote are no more than.; 'that of i;ordlilalisbury to stir. the masses of the elee- • tors into entliusialin for the came of COnservatisni. The magzittade Of the lossythetonservative party has sustainekty the death of Lord Beaconsfield is more andmore'realised ISS one begins to ocinsider who 'his successor must be. His policy was, as we believe, false, flashy, anddisastroure; but that his talent for party leadership amounted to genius, those who watched 'his procedure most intently will be most ready to assert. Lord Beaconsfield was incomparably the tcl3leBt -governing politician his party clld boast for many years before his -death. His defeat at the elections inIS6S and in 'lBBO are no evidence against that extraordinary ability. Naked Toryism can never be otherwise than detestable in the sight of the great bulk of electors of the trading and industrial classes, , and the wonder is met that in spite of the shining ; gloss With which Lord Beaconsfield eoveredthe surface ',. of obsolete Tory notions, the party he led was deci- sively worsted in those memorable encounters, but 'that all his aptitude in beguiling the thoughtless sufficed to gain the Conservative victory of 1874.

div.head: 'LOCAL' NOTES.
div.p: 'LOCAL' NOTES.

Complaints are frequently being made of the prevalence of tramps in th 43 neighbourhood, whose actions are not always of that character which is pleasant to those who live in the outskirts. These fellows call•at ho ma and ask for alms when, if they find that the only occutigillis a ser- vant or the proprietress, they refuse to leave until money is given them, and by dint of threats and intimidation effect their purpose. One of these "wastrels of society" visited the house of a friend the other day where the lady soon 'sent him about his business by a little pardonable duplicity, or what some folks would call strategy. She was alone in the house when a burly-looking tramp called and asked for assistance. Upon her declining to give him any money he placed his foot against thE door, and firmly refused to leave unless she gave him a shilling. Al- though in considerable fear, she retained her presence of mind in a remarkable manner. Without moving from the door she called out to an imaginary man in the adjoining apartment," John, come here, quick; there's a man here who refuses to go unless I give him-some money. Come quick!" In less than a minute the tramp had departed. A landlord possessed of a praiseworthy desire to protect his own property, and to protect the lives of those good people who reside in his houses, has -sent round to each of his tenants a polite request "that no lamp should be used without a chimney, as the smoke spoils the paper and ceiling, and it is also unhealthy." flow lovingly is this landlord?s solicitude for the health of his tenants shown!

The other day when the East wind was blowing very keenly, I,saw an elderly gentleman walking along one of our principal streets with his hand comfortably encased in a sealskin muff. The next day I observed a second gentleman similarly protected at the railway station. This leads me to enquire whether it is to be the fashion nextwinter for gentle- men to carry muffs? Perhaps some of my lady readers who carefully study the latest gossip from Paris and else- where, may be able to throw some light on the subject. It's an ill wind that blows good M no one, and inversely it may be said that a good wind mayhlow harm to some- body. I heard a lament this week—the funniest mixture of the comic and the sorrowful that I have ever heard. it came from an undertaker. I asked him how business was. "Bad, awfully bad," said he; " tell you it isn't possible for a decent tradesman to make a living in these days." "Well, yes," I replied, "the death rate is improving." "Improving," he cried, "there's a great deal too much improvement going on in this town. What with improvements here and improve- ments there it will come that the people won't die at all after a while." This was said quite seriously, and the speaker really appeared to feel the painfulness of his regec- tion. It certainly-may turn out to be a bad job for the un- dertakers, but I think that most of my readers will rejoice if the local sanitary authorities can go on "improving here and improving there" until these gloomy gentlemen, like Othello, find their occupation gone. The idea of a man lamenting in mournful tones that his neighbours and fellow- townsmen are living a little longer than they used to do be- cause their increased longevity deprives him of stew pounds a year is about the most comical idea I have yet come aerol39.

Passing by a well-known public-house the other evening, I had an opportunity of witnessing the careful censorship, which .that much-abused individual—the lidensed victualler —sometimes exercises over his customers. Boniface was standing in the doorway when a gentleman who had evi- dently been freely imbibing attempted to enter, but was promptly stopped by the landlord. "You can't go in here." "Why not ? " queried the bibulous one. "I cannot let you in, that's enough," rejoined Boniface. "D' you mean t' say Pm—hic—drunk ?" continued the other. "Nothing of the sort • just—hic--bad a glass with a friend—hic—see me walk; I'm all right—look here." Of all the failures I ever witnessed that too indulgent gentleman's attempt to prove Ws character for sobriety was the saddest. With faltering steps he travelled a circuitous pilgrimage of about five yards and then made a sudden dash for that haven of refuge of the unstable bibulous—the lamp post— but missing that he grakef Lilly subsided upon the kerb stone. If such were merely the result of "having a glass with a friend," I should not like to see that man's ideal conception of a state of thorough intoxication. LFLACCUS.

WrONES CATIIOL/C DALL.—This annual reunion took place in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Monday evening. There were eOO people present, and dancing commenced at nine o'clock, to the strains of Powell's string band. Mr. John Tallon acted as master of the cerernoaies; Mr. Joha Quinn was president; Mr. John Wheeler treasurer ; and Mr. S. Quinn secretary to the Ball Committee. The proceeis will be devoted to the building fund of the projected new school premises.

Rtnecome Rrnut SANITARY AirritonlTY.—The first meeting of the newly constituted authority, was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Present: Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs J. Knowles, J. Derbyshire, J. Challoner, H. Neild, R. Ashton, J. Mclntyre, P. Percival, and H. Linaker (clerk). The ap- portionmeitt of the cost of the Frodsham sewerage.—The clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board which stated that they had had under their consideration, the re- port made by the inspector, Mr. Smith, after the enquiry held by him relative to the appeal made against the ap- portionment of the expense of constructing sewerage works between the lordship and township of Frodsham • Ind the Board were of opinion that the apportionment made by the authority was a fair and equitable one, subject the follow- ing modification—that the cost of the increase in size of the main sewer in the township, which was necessary in order to convey the sewage of the lordship, as well as that of the township should be borne by the lord- ship. With this alteration the apportionment of the expenses (n,sao 155.) would be £3,118 15s. 4d. to the township, and £761 19s. 86. to the lordship ; and the Board would issue an order apportioning the amount in this manner. When the I order was issued the Board would sanction the necessary loans. Mr. J. G. Bride (medical officer) reported that during the year ending March 1881, the registrar's returns recorded 148 births .ind 86 deaths in the three districts comprised in the TJnion. Of the births 90 were males and 58 females. Of the deaths 40 were males and 46 females, 26 were under 5 years and 19 of these were under 1 year, and GC were five years and upwards. This was all the business.

THZ 'BISHOP OF MANCHESTER ON TUE GOVERNMENT POLICY.—The Bishop of Manchester, preaching on Monday to a crowded congregation in Christ Church, Newgate-street, London, said it was highly creditable to this age of free institutions that the Prime Minister had had the courage of his convictions, and had saved the nation from further crime and blood-guiltiness by reversing the policy of his predeces- sors, and undoing the wrong which had been committed in the Transvaal. Referring to the perils and difficulties by which the commonwealths of Europe were beset, the Bishop said that they could not be remedied by draconian measuree. Nihilism in Russia and Socialism in Germany could not he effectually stamped out under the iron heel of military des- potisin while the people were deprived of the right of free institutions, equal government, and beneficent laws, such as were happily enjoyed in this country. PRESENTATION ar WARRINGTON. —A re-union of the Isle of Mona Lodge (457) of the Order of Druids, was held at the Rose and Crown Inn, Bridge-street, Warrington, on Saturday. Advantage was taken of the occasion to present Bro. Booth, who has held the office of secretary for 28 years, with a handsome eight day time piece, as a token of the respect which the members of the lodge regard his services. P.A. David Hughes (president of the lodge) occupied the chair. The usual toasts having been given, P.D.M. Thomas Leather made the presentation, speaking in felicitious terms of Bro. Booth's services. The recipient suitably replied. It . was stated in the course of the speeches that the total worth of the lodge at the present time was £lBB 195. There had been £5B 15s. paid during the year to sick members, and £3O paid for deaths which had taken place. They had now 98 members. The value of the district funeral fund was £880; the orphans' fund £51.0 10s. 70., and the family funeral fund £5 15s.

Loss OF ,A RIINOORN Sonoma. The schooner Cheshire Lass, of which Mr. S. Ravenscroft, of Runcorn, was managing owner, was sunk on the 1501 inst. The vessel was commanded by Captain Ellis, of Runcorn, and had a crew of five men, all belonging to that port. She was bound from Dublin to Runcorn with a cargo of timber. When off the Skerries she came in collision with the Spanish steamer named Calliengo, outward bouud from the Mersey to Santander. The schooner was damaged to such an extent that she sank immediately after the collision. When news of the disaster first reached Runcorn there was some alarm as to the-safety of the crew. These fears how- ever, were allayed by a telegrrm received by Mr. Ravens- croft, informing him that the crew had succeeded in getting on board the steamer. The men were landed at Santander on Tuesday morning. •

PRESENTATION TO i FAUN:WORTH SCHOOLMISTRESS.-011 it being announced that Miss Crossley, who for 26 years has occupied the position of mistress of the National Girls' Schools at Farnworth, had decided to resign her appoint- ment, a number of parishioners expressed their wish that a suitable testimonial should be given her as a mark of their esteem for her meritorious and long services in the cause of education. A fund was at once opened, and was most spontaneously and liberally subscribed to by about 130 re- sidents in and near Farnworth. The presentation was made on Tuesday, when Miss Crossley was invited to a social gathering held in the girls' school room. The proceedings commenced with tea, at which about 70 of Miss Crossley's friends were present. A musical entertainment followed, and during the interval the presentation was made. The testimonial took the form of a valuable silver tea and coffee service, accompanied by an address, in the latter the parishioners expressed their deep sorrow at Miss Crossley leaving the parish, and their great indebtedness to her for her work in the cause of education in Farnworth. There was another present given by the scholars, which took the form of a handsome glove and handkerchief case.—The Vicar, the Rev. G. Holloway, made the presentation on be- half of the subscribers, and in 'doing so remarked on the very efficient manner in which Miss Crossley during her 26 years' labour in the parish ha,d always discharged her duties, and at the very general regret at her leaving the parish.—Mr. Robert Whalley appropriately returned thanks on behalf of Miss Crossley.—The Rev. S. A. Spooner • and Mr. J. W. Davies also paid a high compliment to Miss Crossley.—Dnring the evening songs and pianoforte solof were given by several ladies and gentlemen connected with the church. SINGULAR CASE OF DROWNING AT Rusconie.—Mr. Ridg- way, coroner, on Wednesday, held an inquest at the Boat- house Hotel, Runcorn, touching the death of James Horan, whose body was found in the Old Quay Dock, Runcorn. Deceased was about twenty-two years of age, and lived with his brother at Weston. A man named Martin Spellman also lived at the same house, and he and the deceased, on Friday night, the Ist of April, went to Runcorn together to bay some articles of clothing. About ten o'clock they went to the Feathers beerhouse, in Church-street, where they had some beer, and left again shortly before eleven o'clock. They were both under the influence of drink, but able to take care of themselves. From the Feathers they went to a house in Mersey-street, occupied by James Higgins. Where a wake was being held on the body of an old man. They remained there,pntil nearly two o'clock the following morn- ing, but accordibg to the evidence of Higgins had nothing whatever to drink, simply chatting end smoking during the whole time. Spellman becoming rather noisy and disposed to interfere with the other persons, he was persuaded by Higgins to go home, and the deceased and he left the house together. Spellman was so much under the influence of drink that he could not remember how he got home, and did not remember parting with Horan, who was not seen alive again, and his body was found in the Old Quay dock on Tuesday afternoon, by a man working en the dock dredge, and it was taken out by P.C. Bossons. When Horan left Higgins's house he was able to walk steadily, and talked all right. The Coroner put several questions to the witnesses as to what opinion they had formed of the manner in which the deceased had met his death, whether by foul means or otherwise, but failed to elicitanything which tended to throw further light on the man's death. A Juror said he thought it was probable that the deceased wished to evade the police in hi, journey to Weston, and had done so by walking along the Old Quay docks, intending to proceed along Irwell-lane, and Heath-road to Weston. Several other jurors concurred in this view, and a verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. COOKERY LECTURE AT Wsuarneirox.—A knowledge of cookery is indispensible to every housewife, not merely on economical grounds, but so that she may be able to pre- pare food in such a manner as to be most wholesome and palatable. Yet this important branch in the education of women is generally the most neglected, many a young wife entering upon her household duties with only a very vague notion of how to prepare the simplest dishes. This should not be so. and it is with the object of imparting some clear ideas on the subject that Mrs. Thwaites, of Liverpool, is giving a series of practical demonstrations in cookery in the National School. The first lecture if the series was given on Wednesday evening to a moderate assemblage of ladies and a few gentlemen. The Rev. W. Quekett occupied the chair, and briefly introduced Mrs. Thwaites to the audience. She performed all her cooking with a gas stove, which she said was v :17 convenient, efficient, and only re- quired a moderate supply of gas. The dishes she prepared were of a medium character, between the very economical and high-class cooking, and were such as might be placed upon the table of a middle-class family any day in the week. They showed how cold meat and scraps of many kinds might he utilised in the prepar.ation of really excellent dishes of an inexpensive character. Her directions and explanations of the processes were very lucid, and with the aide a note book and pencil, which many of the ladies pos- sessed, much valuable information and recipes were to be obtained. The dishes she had prepared were sold at the close of the lecture, and were as follow :—Mock turtle soup, mackerel a /a Normandie, several cold meat dishes, rissoles, and cocoa pudding. Mrs. Thwaites also made some beef tea, giving some hints as to the flavouring, dic., of food intended to be consumed by an invalid. At the conclusion, the Chair- man said many of them would have derived a great deal of knowledge in cookery. He used to be a great man for cookery, and he did exactly as Mrs. Thwaites. He was taught by the great French cook Soyer, who at one time superintended a soup house he had built when in London. He was astonished, and thought the cook was going to make a muddling mess, when be began to put into the great cauldron about three pounds of lard, and then when it was boiling tumble in all the meat and vegetables. That soup was, however, very popular, and he used to sell it at a peany la quart. He had tried to do something similar in Warring- ' ton, and they made the soup the same way. He hoped that Mrs. Thwaite's lectures would be proitable, and that the people of Warrington would give their attention to them, for it would be an advantage to all, as it was very needful that everything they ate should be very well cooked. The lectures were very interesting, and he hoped they would each in their own domestic sphere mention the matter, and they would have a crowded house on the next occasion. Tx a REY. PETER McKnerzus AT ST. HELENS.— The members and congregation of the Wesleyan Methodist community at Nutgrove made an effort on behalf of their proposed new chapel, on which we commented in a former issue. They secured the services of the popular preacher and lecturer the Rev. Peter McKenzie, of Leeds, who preached in the Town Hall in the afternoon to a large con- gregation, from the text "Christ is all in all." A collection was taken at the close. In the evening the rev, gentleman delivered his popular lecture on " Balaam and Balak ; a perverted prophet, and a baffled being." The Mayor (Aid. Harrison) presided, and there was also on the platform the Revs. J. A. B. Harry, W. Q. Pascoe, and R. Crozier; Dr. McNicoll, Messrs. E. Pennington, John Foulkes, Charles Johnson, J. T. Anderton, John Anderton, Br qritchieon, A. Jones and there were also present In the body of the hall Councillors Swift and Walker Mr. IL L. Riley, &c.—The Mayor in his opening remarks said he understood the present chapel was much too small for the requirements of the neighbourhood. The present chapel was now about seventy years old, and since its erection, the increase in the population had ren- dered necessary a more commodious structure, for the build- ing of which it was proposed to raise £2,000. Towards that sum £914 had been subscribed or promised.—The Rev. Peter McKenzie then delivered his lecture, and delineated the character of the prophet and king in his own inimitable manner, which drew from the audience repeated outbursts of applause. The lecture was delivered in an earnest manner, enlivened by frequent flashes of wit and humour.-- Dr. McNicoll moved a vote of thanks to the lecturer and Mayor. They had listened to the lecture with great delight, and, he trusted, with profit. In his own graphic way the lecturer had condensed for them the whole biography of Baalam and the history of the times in which he lived. He had given them an historical picture (a sort of fresco), and had interspersed the lecture with humour, and let loose the lightenings of his eloquence upon the soul filling that place with triumphs. The Mayor, though belonging to another sect, though not another faith, had in the liberality of his mind taken the chair, and filled it satisfactorily.—The reso- lution was adopted, and the compliment was acknowledged by the Chairman and Lecturer. TRH IMPRISONMENT OF THE REV. S. F. GREEN. Among the more interesting of the vestry meetings held on Tuesday was that in connection with the church of St. John the Evangelist, Miles Platting. It was Announced that on Easter Sunday the offerings made in the church on behalf of the imprisoned rector (the Rev. S. F. Green) amounted to £l4O. A resolution was passed protesting that the !aro- ceedings taken against the rector were manifestly unjust, thanking him for his endeavours to preserve to the congre- gation their rights and liberties, and expressing sympathy with Mrs. Green in her present distress. The CLERK laid before the Board his account for conduct- ing the election at Warrington, which amounted to £74 16s. Bd. He had had to prepare 5,409 additional voting papers, and that addition was a greater number than the nnolinf a voters on any question that had been sub- mitted by the corpoi:tion to the ratepayers, and yet for that addition he only got 15's. He thought if they allowed him £2O it was well earned money. Rev. J. YONGE remarked that voting papers had been signed and filled up, when the persons to whom they were addresed had been dead for some months.

The CLERK said he could perhaps explain how that Was. The qualification was 12 months' rating. The rate books were up in two parts—March and September. He went to the overseers' office, and the latest rate book he could obtain was the September one, and there might be the name of a person in the September rate book wild had died. That he could not help, and he had to send a paper to the house. It was of course an impropriety to put a name to a voting paper, and an offence punishable by law. Rev. J. THE MASTER'S REPORT. The MASTER reported that the number of inmates last week was 485; admitted since, 6; discharged, 193; dead, 1; total, 297; as against 466 in the corresponding week of last year. There had been 199 vagrants relieved during the Week, of whom 156 were men, 26 women, and 17 children. The matron begged to acknowledge with thanks the r.ceipt of a basket of flowers for the sick from the Rev. B. B. Prescott. On behalf of the inmates of the institution, the master wouldlike to kindly thank the ladies and gentlemen who gave their services at the concert on Tuesday night, and contributed to all spending so enjoyable an evening. 1 THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE POOR LAWS. , A letter Was read from the Local Government Board acknowledging receipt of the Guardians' letter .of the 2nd inst., forwarding a memorial containing certain suggestions with reference to the administration of the Poor Laws, and stating that the memorial would receive the consideration of the Board.

THE HOSPITAL EXTENSION. A letter was also read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the expenditure of the sum of £5OO in carrying out the works in connection with the extension of the fever hospital at the workhouse. THE DISPUTE WITH THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of the Guardians' letter of the 10th ult., and forwarding for the information of the ' Guardians copy of a communication which the Board had that day (April 13) addressed to the Newton Improvement Commissioners on the subject of their letter of the 251 h of February last. The copy communication was as follows : "I am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to your letter with reference to the question of the pro- vision by hospital accommodation of means of isolation in the case of poor persons suffering from infectious disease, and to forward for the information of the improvement com- missioners for the district of Newton-in-Makerfield the en- closed copy of a letter which the Board have received front the Guardians of the Warrington Union, with whom they have been in communication on the subject. As regards the questions upon which the improvement commissioners are desirous of obtaining the opinion of the Board, I am directed to state that the Board consider that as a general rule when any person attacked with fever, or any cantagious or infectious disease (whether the case occurs within the dis- trict of an urban sanitary authority, or within that of a rural sanitary authority), is without the moans of obtaining such necessaries (inMuding medical attendance and nursing) as be may require, it devolves upon the guardians of the Union or their officers to afford the rcquisite relief. If, however, the removal of a patient to a hospital is only necessary for the purpose of isolation, and the person is not destitute, either wholly or to the extent above referred to, the Board are of opinion that it devolves upon the sanitary authority of the district, and not upon the Guardians, to deal with the case."

Mr. WINSTANLKT : That confirms my opinion. The CLERK, in reply to a Guardian, said the bill had not been paid, but he hoped after that letter the Newton Com- missioners would pay it. Mr. DARBYSRIRE said it should be remembered the Guardians took the cases in for isolation only, and not be- cause they were paupers. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: WEST CIIESIIIRE ELECTION.
div.p: WEST CIIESIIIRE ELECTION.

On Saturday, the nomination of candidates for the Wes- tern Division of Cheshire took place at Chester. James Tomkinson (Liberal), of Wellington Hall, Tarporley, was proposed by Lord Richard Grosvenor, and seconded by Sir Thomas Gibbons Frost; Henry James Tollemache (Con- servative), of Dorfolk Hall, Nantwich, was proposed by Cudworth Salstead Poole, of Marbury Hall, near Whit. church, and seconded by Thomas Finchett, of Rushton, Cheshire. Meetings have been held in all parts of the con- stituency during the week, which have been addressed by both candidates, and Mr. Tomkinson has been rec eived heartily. On Thursday, the candidates for West Cheshire concl laded their canvass. The Liberal candidate (Mr. Tomkinson) I visited a number of places in the Birkenhead district, addressing meetings at Sutton and West Kirby. Mr. Tolle- mache directed his attention :to the easterly part of the division, and spoke at gatherings at Nantwich and Crewe, where he was supported by a powerful body of members of Parliament and others, among them being Mr. Stavely Hill, M.P., Mr. Bromley-Davenport, M.P., Mr. W. F. Tollemache, M.P., and in the evening, the Right Hon. Lord George , Hamilton, M.P.

A public meeting of the electors of Wiasford and its vicinity was convened in the Town Hall, under the presi- dency of Mr. J. Slater, on Tuesday night, to hear Mr. J. Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate. As his spirited address had taken hold of their hearts, it only required a fuller exposition to settle the affair, as far as Winsford there represented was concerned, as to who should go for this division of the county. The ball was crowded. On the platform were various local gentlemen ; and in addition to Messrs. A. J. Mclntyre, Q.C., M.P., W. Y. Craig, M.P., G. W. Latham, J.P.,J. Tomkinson, J.P., R. Stubbs, J. H. Cooke, John Cooke, J. Hewitt, the Rev. T. Naylor (Northwich), J. T. Maxwell, and a host of others, whose speeches were warmly received and loudly cheered, as point after point was touched upon of the different parts of home and foreign policy of the ministry Mr. Tomkinson would support. The resolution of support of Mr. Tomkinson's candidature was carried with acclamation. The meeting was through out most enthusiastic.

div.head: POLLING YESTERDAY.
div.p: THE POLLING YESTERDAY.

_ Throughout the whole of the district both parties strove to bring up their supporters to the poll, and reports were re- ceived during the day that polling proceeded rapidly with- out disorder. The Conservatives engaged more cabs than the Liberals, so large a number being taken from Warring- ton that no cabs cabs could be got during the day in Warrington. It is alleged that in the Tarporley division a large number of voters, who last year supported Sir Philip Egerton, yesterday recorded votes for the Liberal candidate. At Crewe there was some excitement, and the Liberal party favours predominated. There are a large number of work- ingmen freeholders in the borough, who would support Mr. Tomkinson. At Nantwich the reports state that party feelinz is pretty evenly divided, and the current runs strongly. A posse of police has been brought into the town to maintain order. At Neston the normal condition of the place was undisturbed, and the best feeling subsisted between the cousin-candidates. One report stated that the farmers were busy with agricultural concerns, and that wo'ed affect the polling. At mid-day at Chester only 300 voters had p!4l Out of a total of 1,200. The poll five o'clock, and the polling boxes were broughtclosecilntaot Chester from all parts of the constituenzr. ins boxes were received at Chester Sto!,'.on, and taken direct to the Grand Jury Room at Chester Castle, where the votes were cast up.

div.head: Majority for the Conservative
div.p: Majority for the Conservative

(SPECIAL TELEGRAM.) CHESTER, FRIDAY 11 p.m.—The West Cheshire Election went off very quietly. No squibs or placarda were em- ployed, and the Conservatives were confident of victory. The result, declared at Cheater Castle at half-past ten, was a considerable source of astonishment to the Conservatives who had anticipated a much larger majority. The election last year resulted in a majority of over seven hundred for the Conservatives, and as the registra- tion had been neglected since then by the Liberals, the latter did not hope for victory. The official numbers were : Henry James Tollemache (C) 4,800, James Tomkinson, (L) 4,418. Majority for the Conservative, 382. More polled this time than last election the register having been largely increased by the ad- dition of Conservatives and the striking off of Liberals. Mr. Tomkinson addressed the electors and said he considered it a great moral victory for the Liberals, and that if selected again he would win the fight in the Liberal interest. (Loud cheers.)

LORD BEACONSFIELD'S FUNERAL.

It has now been finally decided that Lord Beaconsfield's funeral shall take place at Rughendeu, en Tuesday next. The remains, it is stated, will he cony ed to Hughendett by road, and the funeral will be co ted in as quiet a manner as possible. The decision may give some disap- pointment to the nation, as it was generally felt that the death of a foremost statesman, who has constantly devoted his genius to the service of the country, should be com- memorated by some formal expression of the nation's sorrow. But the terms of the ex-Premier's will were 80 explicit that the decision of his executors to adhere to thetk will meet with general approval. The Court Circular, on Thursday, records that Lord Rowton had an interview with her Majesty, and communicated to the Queen "the touching details of the last hour of her Majesty's,valued friend, Lord Beaconsfield."

The following notice was issued last night:—Lord. Beaconsfield's executors desire to announce that, in de- ference to wishes so deafly expressed by his lordship, his ..funeral will be conducted as privately as possible, and ad- mission to Hughenden-Manbr will necessarily ke extremely, limited. But inasmuch as many of Lord Beaconsfield's, friends may desire to be preient at the ceremony which will. take place in the churchyaid at half-past three o'clock on, Tuesday, the executors think it right to state that the Great' Western Railway Company ha:e ;made arrangements to =- special trains from Paddington on that day.

THE PRESTON MURDER. Two youths, James Hunter and Alfred Foster were com- mitted for trial at Preston, yesterday, for the wilful murder . of William Eccleston, whom they kicked to death, ea Saturday last, upon his interfering to protect a woman they were illtreating.

I EASTER MONDAY AT WARSIIWTON.—Tbe town prri, sented a most deserted appearande on Easter Monday. J3eing• Bank Holiday as well, the business establishments were closed, and the inhabitant betook themselves in large num- bers to the various places of popular resort in the neigh- bourhood. The day was beautifully -fine, but was very cold owing to the east wind which prevailed during the day.

THE DEATH OF LORD BEACONSFIELD.—The inhabitants of Warrington, in common with those of the whole of the kingdom, were startled on Tuesday morning to learn of the death of Lord Beaconsfield. The news of the sad event was posted in front of the Examiner Office, and was eagerly scanned by large numbers of persons who, however, could scarcely believe that the ex-Premier had passed away. The arrival of the evening papers confirmed the mournful in- telligence, which then became the subject of general con- versation, and persons of all shades of political opinion ex- pressed their sincere regret at the sad event. The flags at the Town Hall and the Conservative Club were hoisted half mast, and on Tuesday evening the bellringers of St. Paul's Church rang a muffled peal.

, WILFUL DAMAGE.—John Clewes, John Ditcl2field, and Frederick Yates were charged with having, on the 25th March, wilfully and maliciously damaged the property of Mr. D. R. Davies, J.P.. by breaking the windows of hie residence.—The damage was laid at ss. Since taking out. the summonses complainant had died, and the Bench had received a letter from the son asking them, under the painful circumstances, to admonish the defendants and discharge them.—Defendants were, therefore, dismissed with a can- , tion.

DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES. William DeWlatlrS4 fustian cutter, was charged with being drunk on the pre- mises of the Green Dragon Inn, Heatley, on the 16th April, and refusing to quit. Joseph Parker, the landlord, deposed to requesting defendant to leave his bowling green, but he refused to do so, and he, therefore obtained the assistance of P.C. Maddock, who forcibly ejected him. Defendant called John Shaw, who stated that the complainant and the de- fendant got "chaffing" on the green, and the complainant, "getting vexed," ordered him off. Fined ss. and 10s. d. costs.—Richard Foster, a young man, was charged with a similar offence on the same day. Complainant stated that the defendant entered his house sober during the afternoon, and he stayed until night. When be considered defendant had had enough drink he refused to serve him with any more, and requested him to leave. Defen- dant was under the influence of drink, and be- came very violent. P.C. Maddock deposed to putting defendant out of the house. He was drunk, and not fit to have any more liquor.—Defendant: Did you say you did not want to lock me up, as you were as drunk as me, and if you went to Lymtn the sergeant would lock you up? (Laughter.l—Witness : No.—Defendant was fined 55., and 13s. 6d. costs.

THE FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—Tbomas Bradbury was charged with, on the 17th instant, causing two cows and a calf to be removed without having obtained the re- quisite license—John Southern was also charged with removing the same.—Defendants pleaded that they were ignorant of the orders, and the Bench believing that to be so, dismissed the case, but ordered them to pay the costs. TEE RECOVERY OF FnrEs.—James Cronis was charged with neglecting to pay a penalty of 10s. imposed upon him on September 17th, 1880, for offences against the Elemen- tary Education Act —Mr. Joseph Toft,the school attendance officer, said he was instructed by the committee to recover the money, or press for defendant's commitment. Mr. Toft said defendant earned 172. per week, and lived at the farm where he worked.—The Bench made an order for the pay- ment of the fine at the rate of le per week.

CONCERT AT LYILM.—On Thursday, the Lymm bras* band gave a vocal and instrumental concert in the Congre- gational Schoolroom. There was a large audience, and the efforts of the instrumentalists and vocalists, which were very successful, were much appreciated. The band played about eight selections, among which were "Fairy Queen," "Valley de Roses." and "Silver Bells." Mr. Hindes con- trOuted "Betsy Wareing" and "Sweet face at the window,' Mr. Moody " Maid of Athens" and "Some day ;" Mr. Alyward "Right or wrong" and "On guard 1684 and 1881;" and Mr. Rigby sang songs entitled " Dutch " and "When she fainted away." The proceeds of the entertain- ment will be added to the funds of the band.

IS THERE NOT A CAUSE? .81r,—About eight months age, in company with the owners of the adjoining property, I received notice to convert the open aahpit attached to my house into the pail system, and, 'ming a law-abiding citizen, I at once complied with the notice. I and my neighbours are the owners of abotit forty houses all in the same block, and, with the exception of two houses, the conversion was completed months ago. What I want to kno as is, how it should happen that the ownet of these two houses should be allowed to set the law at de4ancs ? and I have been wondering whether "there is not a cause." May be the owner is a member of the Cor- poration, or an official connected therewith. I don't know if this be so, but this much I do know, that if the Mayor or any other member of the Corporation had been seated in my house one evening last week when these two remaining open aehpits were emptied, he would have sworn by all that was good, bad, or indifferent, that such a stench as was emitted should not be tolerated any longer. If there is any- thins to bring the sanitary laws of the borough into dis- favour, it is making fish of one and flesh of another.—l am, yours, &c., ORDER.

SATIIRDAY.—Before Mr. F. W. Earle. THE ROBBERY AND OUTRAGE AT WHISTON.—John Lewis, alias John Savage, a Welshman, was brought up on remand I charged with having, at Whiston, on the 19th March, stolen .3.55. from the person of Henry Laurenson, a man nearly 70 years of age ; and also with afterwards unlawfully and vio- lently assaulting him.—On the Saturday night in question the old man went into the Green flagon I'm, Warrington - road, Walston, and whilst there pasoner rifled his pockets of their contents: On finding that he had been robbed, prosecutor left the house. On his way home he was over- taken and attacked by the prisoner, who struck him and knocked him down, and afterwards dragged him into a mad- house on the Royal Oak Farm, and locked the door on the outside. Newt morning the poor old fellow was found by one of the servants in a very weak and ex- hausted state. He was removed to his home, and medical assistance obtained. He was confined to his bed for several days in consequence of the brutal treatment he had received, and was for some tims in a dangerous con- dition.—On being formally charged, prisoner said he was guilty of robbing the old man, but emphatically denied having assaulted him.—lt was stated that the prisoner was an old offender, baying been previously convicted several times for felony.—Ha was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. Before Mr. W. L. Evans. DISORDERLY CONDUCT IN THE WORKHOLTSE.—George Hughes, a tramp, who described himself as a blacksmith, of Chorley, was charged with disorderly conduct at the Whis- ton Workhouse, on the previous Thursday night. Prisoner was let into the vagrant ward at the Workhouse about eight o'clock, and, about half an hour afterwards, the porter hear- ing a disturbance in the w4rd, went thither, and found the prisoner had been assaulting another tramp named Thomas Owen, who was lying on the floor .01a bleeding from a wound which he had received. Prisoner was then given into cusrody.—On being asked if bad anyth'ng to say the priso- ner said he bad only struck Owen in set f-defence.—He was sent to gaol for fourteen days with hard laboutt.
