Lord Beaconsfield was an honorary D.C.L. of Oxford and Edinburgh, a Privy Councillor, a Trustee of the British Museum, a Governor of Wellington College, an Elder Brother of the Trinity House, a Trustee of the National Portrait Gallery) and a Deputy-Lieutenant for Bucks and was a Royal Commissioner of the Great Exhibition of 1851. He was installed Lord Rector of the University of aiaegow November 19, 1873, and reelected to that office in November,lB74. ' Having briefly mentioned the principal incidents in the life of Lord Beaconsfield, we need only conducte the sketch wwoarsd ss age ce ne sesrfaul yi na s thatt o hish mp rpo de ruscotni oa st yh.a e bAesena nbyoveal ifsetwh e most extensively read. That they are of the best order of literary performanceshasbeen doubted by critics thoroughly impartial and well able to form a just opinion. As a poll:- dal...an, while it would be idle for the strongest partisan to deny that he will leave his mark behind him, and deserve ' the prominent recognition of the historian of the nineteenth I century, he was not so successful as political success should 14,4 counted. It has been well said:—" Except the Royal itles Rill, there. is no measure which Mr. Disraeli has ear- ned lathe form In which he originally framed it. The great Acts which bear his name, were they not stolen from his predecessors? We do not charge him with any con- scious dishonesty in this. He himself has said that the whole history of politics proves that great measures, have heen passed only when the party that framed them liaia been defeated upon them, and been succeeded by their opponents. But we do not claim that on this we can charge him with the want of original statesmanship or the genius` of a philosopher. He has enunciated no new principles. has carried none into practice. On the other hand, he haS been a close student of history, a clever observer of men: lie has believed all to depend on the influence of indivi- dual 'character.' English political history knows of no statesman so successful when he chose in the appointment of right men to the right places. He has been equally ex- pert in drawing, models for himself, He has studied and successfully imitated nearly every great English statesman. He has ehuffled into other men's aims and policies v,fithont, number. His political wardrobe is a repository of political i ~ old clothes. has worn each suit of them with great: advantage to himself, with some benefit to his party, wltty. none to his country. Into discarded politics he has info his Wondelf al personal vigour. But the strength both e his measures and of the general position into which he has led his party will pass away with himself. His retirement from politics will be follewed by a relapse of the Conserve- Rya into Toryism. He has been all along the foreign element in the Conservative body, working slowly to his own ejection."

THE FUNERAL. A proposal that the remains of the Earl of Beaconsfield ihould be interred with public honours in Westminster Abbey was made by Mr. Gladstone immediately after he re- ceived the melancholy news of the death of the noble Earl. It appears. however, that the terms of Lord Beaconsfield's will prevenchis executors from complying with the request which expressed the general feeling of the nation. Several years ago, Lord Ileaconsfield directed that his remains should be buried in the same vault with thoile of his de- ceased wife "Mary Anne Disraeli, created in her own right Viscount 'Beaconsfield," and he further desired that his • funeral should be conducted "with the same simplicity as hers was." A telegram'was received in Curzon-street on Wednesday morning, commanding the attendance of Lord Rowton at Osborne House, and his lordship obeyed the summons at once. It was understood that her Majetty de- sired to see Lord Rowton in order to communicath her wishes ' as to the funeral. The funeral will probably take place on Tuesday next. It is noted as a remarkable coincidence that Lord Beaconsfield died on the anniversary of the day on which he surrendered to her Majesty, at Windsor, for tire second time, the seals of office. The leading journals in all the continental capitals have published elaborate notices of the deceased peer in his qualities of statesman and author. The German and Austrian journals are especially cnrdial in their recognition of his talents. Some of the New York newspapers comment on his career. At Ottawa the flags on the public buildings have been lowered to half- mast.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. G. Artingstall, and Mr. John Rylands. EXCESSITE EMPLOYMENT OF A Caltrzn.—Michael Tans - ley was charged with being asleep in charge of a horse and cart, in Warrington-road, Penketh, at eleven o'clock on the 12th inst.—Defendant pleaded guilty, but said be had been working continuously for two days and two nights. He stated he was employed by Mr. Grace.—The Chairman said that firm appeared to keep their 'carters working night and day, and asked if they would pay the fine for defendant.— Defendant said they would not, and he was fined 2s. 61. and costs. OFFENCES AGAINST THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT.—Charles Brassey was charged with removing three cows along the highway at Penketh, on the 7th inst., with- out having obtained a certificate. Defendant appeared to have been labouring under a mistake, and the Bench dis- missed the case.—For a similaroffence committed in Sankey, •

Samuel Shaw was ordered to pay casts. SCEOOL ATTENDANCE PROSECUTIONS.—Peter Lygoe was ' charged with neglecting to send a child named Martha Tay- I lor, of which he was the guardian, regularly to school. Mr. ' Hobson said that the child had only made 47 out of '5B I possible. Defendant said the child was sick, and the doctor / was in attendance upon her. Fined 53 and cost..—Jobn I Muskett was similarly charged in respect to his on Wm., who had been absent 191 times from school. Mr. Hobson I asked for an order for the boy's attendance at school, and .1 the Bench made the order. For not sending his son Charles to schocl, in compliance with, an order, Albert Smith was fined b.—Enoch Hewitt was summoned for not sending his daughter, Margaret Ellen, to school. Defendant said the child was delicate, and as the distance to .the school was over two miles it was impossible for her to go in bad weather. Adjourned a month to allow defendant to send his daughter to school.—John Higham was similarly sum- moned. His daughter Ann had had only made 220 atten- dances out of a possible 443. Defendant.said the child was in delicate health and was not fit to go to school, which was about three miles distant. She had to start from home at eight o'clock in the morning, and, when the weather was rough. had to sit in school until five o'clock at night. The attendances of the girl had not always been marked, as on several occasions she had been unable to answer to her name, and the schoolmaster when he had seen her had called her "a Houghton Green bull dog."—Mr. Hobson asked for an adjournment of the case to ascertain if this statement was true.—Adjourned for a month. THEFT Of, PlGEorrs.--Edward Tuckwell (18) was charged with stealing two pigeons of the valde of 2s„ lki., the pro- pert,' of Wm. Gosling, of Orford.—Prosecaor saw the pigeons safe in the cote about 6 o'clock on Friday, the 15th instant, but on the follovring morning two of the pigeons were missing. He went to Warrington and found them at the house of Mrs. Locker, who bad purchased them from the prisoner.—Prisoner Pleaded guilty, and stated that be worked at Dallam Forge, and had only been in Warrington about three weeks.—Fined 10s. including costs.

IRON AND COAL TRADES. LiNCASIIIRE.—The coal trade of this district is _without any very material change from last week, business to a con- siderable extent having been interfered with, by the Easter holidays which have entailed a cessation of work for several days at most of the collieries and ironworks througb. out the district. In the Manchester distriet•the principal colliery firms continue well supplied with orders and late rates are maintained, but in the outside districts and through- out West Lancashire business generally is reported to be dull, and at many of. the pits considerable stocks are accumulating. Although there is no very Material quotable change in prices, the tendency, so far as all classes of round coal are concerned, is downwards, and in some cases sellers are now quoting prices quite as low as those ruling prior to the late strike. For the better classes of round coal a fair inquiry is still maintained, but the common sorts, owing to the depression in the shipping trade and the limited demand for iron making and other manufacturing purposes, are being pushed upon the market for house-fire purposes at very low figures. Inquiries are now coming into the market for gas. making coals, and for contracts over the next twelve months comparatively low prices are being quoted, but colliery pro- prietors generally are disinclined to enter into engagements over more extended periods. For engine fuel there is a tolerably good demand, and prices are firm, with a tendency to stiffen so far as the better qualities of slack are concerned, and this, notwithstanding that burgy is generally abundant the market, is tending to keep up the price of this description of fuel. The average prices at the pit mouth remain about as under. Best coal, 9s. to Os. 6d.; seconds, 7s. 6d.; common coals, ss. 3d. to SS. Pd.; burgy, 4s. 6d. to 55.; good slack, 4s. up to 4s. 9d. with common sorts averaging about 3s. to 3s. 6d. per ton. There is very little inquiry for coal for shipment, and, to ' secure cargoes, very low prices are being quoted. In the iron trade of this district there is still no sign whatever of any improvement, and the spring having adianced without the anticipated revival in trade being realised, the market for the present seems to have collapsed. The recent quarterly meetings have brought- no accession of new business, fewer, orders having resnited from them than has been known for a long time past. For pig iron the demand is extremely quiet,. consumers and Merchants only purchasing small par-1 ' eels as their requirements compel them to come into the mar- ket, and it seems questionable whether any concessiens in prices would bring forward business unless sellers were to spread deliveries over extended periods. For Lanca- shire pig iron delivered into the Manchester district, quota- lions rennin nominally at 455. for No. 4 forge and 465. per for No. 3 foundry, less n per cent, with makers open to 'offers. Very few sales,,however, are reported, and stocks are 'Accumulating. In outside brands the tendency of prices is ieasier, but there bas been nothing doing to test actually the :lowest figures which sellers would be willing to take. Manu- factured iron is 'only in 'very limited demand, with prices *easier, bars delivered into: the Manchester distriet being quoted Ifat from £5 12s. 6d. to £.5 155., and for good specifications for Ilprompt delivery even lower figurell than these woul& prob- !ably be accepted in some cases.

A BAPTIST CHAPEL FOR EARLES- TOWN. LAYING THE FOUNDATION STONE. The Baptists of Earlestown have decided to erect a place of worship, and on Monday the first step towards giving effect to this decision was taken in the laying of the foun- dation stone. The Baptists, as a body, have not been very long in existence in Earlestown. They commenced, like many other Nonconformist churches which now occupy pro- minent positions, by hiring a room in which to conduct their services; and here they have laboured for ten years. Sue- cess attended the efforts put forth, and the members began to consider the desirability of having a chapel, with the re- sult that preliminary steps were taken with a view to raise funds to carry out their project. A sufficlant sum was realised to warrant their proceeding with the erection of an edifice, and an eligible site was secured in Crown-st., imme- diately off Market-street. The structure will consist of the chapel, which will be 54 feet by 33 feet, together with two vestries each 15 feet by 12 feet 6 inches, and a large class room 32 feet by 15 feet 6 inches. It will be built in the. Gothic style, of grey Gersten bricks with dressings of red pressed Rainhill bricks; while the rostrum, pews, &c., win be of pitch pine. The chapel will be heated with hot air apparatus, and artificially lighted with gas. The building, which is to seat about 300 persons, is estimated to coet about £l,lOO, and towards that amount about £650 is already in hand. The work has been commenced by Mr. Edward Davies, the builder, and the ceremony of laying the founda- tion stone took place as above stated on Monday. The weather was most auspicious, and a large number of people assembled to witness the ceremony. The Rev. H. Stowell Brown, of Liverpool, had been announced to lay the stone, but at the last moment a telegram was received from the rev, gentleman stating that he could not be present, and his place was taken by Mr. W. P. Lockhart, of Liverpool. Amongst these present were the Revs, G. W. N. Carey, S. Hawkes, Liverpool; W. Filling, Hill °Rife, Warrington ;T. Wilshaw,St. Helens; R. Crozier, and W. C. Tayler ; Meassa. J. Harrison, Isaac Miller, IT,. B. Wealthy, Weaver, R. M. Marricott, H. Golding, dm. The ' proceedings commenced with the singing of the hymn" All bail the power of Jesu's' name," and after prayer by the Rev. R. 'Crozier, The Rev. W. C. TATLBR addressed the assembly. He said that to those who were more immediately concerned in the building whose foundation stone they were about to lay, that day was one of great gladness and joy. They had hitherto been without a house of their own wherein they, might worship their God. They had longed, and prayed, and worked for a house, and that day what did their eyes see ? The walls of a building rising up within which they would sing hymns of praise, making melody in their hearts to God—would pray unto the Lord and Father of their Lord Jesus Christ, and would have the presence and blessing of their Divine Master. That day they saw the beginning of the end of that for which they , had long prayed and worked, and their hearts were joyous, 'and their language was "Bless the Lord, 0 our souls, and all that is within us bless His Holy Name. Bless the Lord, 0 our souls, and forget not all His benefits." They who' built that house were known among men as Baptists. They, in common with other professed Christians, recognized that Christ was the only head of and sovereign in the church, and because they obeyed Him as their head and bowed to Him as their sovereign, as it regarded their particular ordinance which He instituted, men had given them that name—Baptists. They did not wish to get rid of the name, for they were not ashamed of it, but rather re- joiced in it. It was their glory just as much as, and even more than, the term Methodist was to the great Methodist body—as Congregationalist was to the Congregational body, and so on. As Baptists, they had a history of which they were justly proud—a history of suffering of persecution, of patient working for Christ, of being in the front ranks con- tending for civil and religions liberty, crying for the free- dom of all enslaved, and carrying to the remotest parts of the earth the glorious gospel of the blessed God. As Bap- tists, too, they had a long ancestry. Some good people in their ignorance thought they were of yesterday, but that was not so. They could trace up their ancestry in an unbroken line to the Apostles and to Christ Himself. For what saith the Scripture of truth? "Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John to be baptised of hist." They were, however, so far as Earlestown was concerned, only of yes- terday. Ten years ago they had no existence. There were, it was true, three or four families who not only held Bap- tist principles, but were truly Baptists. But they might have been Mormons or anything else for what the town knew of them. However, before the close of 1871, some of the Baptists thinking they had hidden their light quite long enotigh under a bushel, deter.nined to take the bushel off that the light might shine forth. They did it in this way: They hired an upper room in Market-street, and then posted the town with bills announcing that on Lord's Day, October 32nd, 1871, the room would be opened for religions worship according to the principles and practices of the Baptists. At first, very little progress was made. The five who started the cause, and those who belonged to them, met ' together, but others did not seem willing to meet with them. , However, in the year 1875 the brethren managed to get under the warm and cozy wing of HI Myrtle-street Bap. I tit Church, Liverpool, and became members of that church, and at the same time they started a Sunday school. From that period progression had been steady and sure, and now there was a church of 40 members, a congregation on Sun- day evenings numbering upwards of 100, and a Sunday I school at which there were 193 scholars in actual attend- ance. Seven years ago the people who met in Market-street began to think of having on some future day a chapel of their own. For the purpose of starting a building fund cards were given to the members to obtain subscriptions, and on July Ist, 1874, the first sum of money thus obtained —£s es.—was brought in. In October, 1879, the amount collected was £192 10s., and last year a bazaar was held, which, with safe of work afterwards, considerably increased the amount. The buildings, an outline of which they now saw, would cost upwards of £l,OOO. Towards that sum they had £4OO. Their friends at Myrtle-street, Liverpool, though they had had their hands full with Princes Park Gate new chapel and their own alterations; had nobly put their hands to the work and contributed £250. Thus they would see more than one-half of the cost was in hand. He then proceeded to make an appeal for help, remarking that it would be evident to all that besides the building they were erecting, they badly wanted a Sunday school room. (Applause.) Mr. LOCKHART then proceeded to adjust the stone, which was lowered into position, and he declared, amid applause, that it bad been "well and truly laid." He remarked that, with regard to the inscription engraved upon the stone, he thought he might truly say it lied—(laughter)—for it declared that it was laid by the Rev. H. Stowell Brown, and nothing of the sort had taken place. He was sure all of them were extremely sorry that the truth which was in, tended to have been spoken on the stone had not been acted out there. (Hear, hear.) They very much regretted the absence of their esteemed friend, Mr. Brown; and they:: earnestly hoped there was no serious cause for his absence from amongst them that day. It was only to be accounted an accident that they had been so kind as to select him (the speaker) to lay the stone that day. It was customary, as they knew, either to select a man of great eminence or a man of considerable wealth to lay the foundation stone of a building such as that. He happened to be neither a man of great eminence nor a man of any considerable wealth; and therefore he believed the accident of his having to lay the stone would not add anything to the lustre of the proceede jogs of that day, as would have been the case had they been favoured with the presence of their esteemed friend, Mt. Brown. He had done the best he could in seeing the stone, was well and truly laid; and it would be for them, when the collection was made, to subscribe the deficiency caused by the absence of Mr. Brown; and he hoped when the col, lection came to be counted it would be found that there was a very considerable reduction of the amount of the dea. ciency which still remained in order to make up the entire cost of the building. He could heartily congratulate his friend Mr. Taylor, whom he had known for a great many years. His memory carried him back to the days when in a building which was then used as a chapel, but which was now used as Turkish baths—(laughter)—Mr. Taylor ' preached his trial sermon before the members of the Baptist chapel, Myrtle-street, previous to going to college to be, educated for the Christian ministry. He heard Mr. Taylor on that occasion with very great pleasure, and he heard him with equal pleasure when he made his lucid statement just now. He heartily congratulated Mr. Taylor and those who were associated with him in this great work on the very great progress they had already male, and he wished all possible blessing to them in connection with the spiritual work in which they were permitted to take part there. Mr. Tayler had said they were Christiana—that was to.say, they believed in the Lord Jesus Christ as the Son of God, and One who came down from heaven to earth that he might be the redeemer of the children of men. They believed in the Holy Scripture, as the authoritative and the inspired revelation of God wherein He made known His will, and revealed His love to mankind; and they believed in the Holy Spirit of one who through His power awakened the dead in trespasses and sins, and led sinners to believe. on the Lord Jesus Christ to the salvation of their souls. Therefore, though they were distinguished by the name of Baptists, they ,eld those prin- ciples and many others to which he could not then allude, in common with the whole church of the Lord Jesus Christ, divided as it was into many different denominations and communities. While they were there as Baptists, he was sure that both Mr. Taylor and those who were associa- ted with him would join with him (Mr. Lockhart) in sayina they were there in no spirit of enmity towards any branch of the Church of Christ. (Hear, hear.) They were there in thorough loving concord with all who loved the same Saviour that they did. They stretched out their hands to other denominations as they trusted others stretched out their hands to them in regard and sympathy, and sought to stand shoulder to shoulder with them in the great work of seeking to extend the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ. Whilst he said this they did of course hold distinctive prin- ciples to which they were called to bear witness in the baptism of believers only—of such as made a creditable profession of their !faith. It seemed to there from their study of the sacred scripture that the ordinance of baptism, like the other ordinance of the Lord's eupper, was designed by the great Head of the Church to be administered only to such as gave sufficient and satisfactory evidence of their having experienced the grace of God. They disclaimed altogether that baptism could save a man, or that baptism was essential to salvation. Don't let them forget while there might he differences of certain points among believers ' 'there were far more points of contact. He was one of those who thought that possibly no one section of the Christian Church contained the whole truth unmixed with error, and and that in all probability each section of the church, as it has been called into being, bad borne witneee to one or more

points of truth which had been overlooked by other sec- tions of the church. While, he hesitated to say that denominationalism was the set purpose of God, he was very strongly inclined to believe that the existence of the various denominations was permitted by God in His infinite wisdom in order that from the existence of them the whole truth might be borne witness to, and not one single point left without the testimony being given in regard to it. The existence of a place of worship, and the building of a new place of worship, seemed to him to be a testimony to all around of the gospel. He was reading the other day as to the measure of the testimony that was being borne by the people of this time. About 400 years ago there were only a few thousand copies of the Word of God in existence. In the year 1800 it was calculated there were newly 4,000,000 copies of the Bible in the whom world ; but in these days there was a new Bible printed every five minutes —in other words, in one year there were printed very nearly as many bibles as existed in the whole world 81 years ago. Now, just as every new chapel bore a testimony to men of the gospel, so every fresh copy of the Word of God which I went forth from the press bore a similar testimony of the ' measage of salvation, and what he wanted to point out was the very solemn responsibility that rested upon every man,,, every woman, and every child that had come to years id ' understanding in this land and in this day of testimony as cn whether they had reeeived or rejected the salvation or' aosl. He concluded by again appealing to the spectators tte supply any deficiency which had been caused by his iaying the stone. A collection was then made, and the proceedings termi- nated. Afterwards a tea meeting was held in the Viaduct Insti- tute, at which about 400 persons sat down, and, their 'appetites having been satisfied, the tables were cleared, and a public meeting was held, over which Mr. Lockhart pre- sided. The Cam-two.; having alluded to the unavoidable absence of the Rev. H. S. Brown, again congratulated Mr. Tayler on the day's proceedings—(hear, hear,)—and also Mr. Aveline—(applause)—who had been for a long time associated with the work in that place. He did not know that any one of them could to the full understand how very much that infant cause owed to the assiduous labours of Mr. Aveline, and he thought they ought all to feel indebted to him fer his efforts to promote the cause. He went on to state how very important it was that they should not let chapel building occupy too prominent a place in their minds, and suggested that when the building, the foundation stone ef which had been laid that day, was completed, they should earnestly pray that they might not be too much occupied with the mere, shell —as a chapel, church, or cathedral, was after all a mere convenience to keep off the weather—but with all their hear, soul, and strength combine their energies to the great spiritual work to which God in His mercy had called them. In conclusion he remarked that the inscription upon the stone had been effaced, and thought that was a symbol that the Baptists of Earlestown had not only a love of truth, but of prompti- tude of action, and he hoped they would always be signalised by a great love of truth and great Ipromptitude of action in the serviae of the Lord. (Applause.) Rev. T. WILSITAR then spoke on Christian fellowship, and the Rev. W. C. TAYLOR gave an interesting history of the es- tablishment of the Baptist cause in Earlestown. After addresses by the Revs. C. W. N. CA.RRY, and S. HAWIEBS, the Rev. W. PILLING said he rejoiced heartily that Baptist' principles were being so rapidly extended in the neighbour- hood of Earlestown. He thought it was a great pity when they looked upon the locality and beheld the rising popula- tion of the various towns in the midst of which they were placed, to see that Baptistprinciples were so little known ; and he thought there was needed that they should combine together with Liverpool, as the weakness and the strength would be better for them all if it could be more united. He was very glad indeed to see that they had laid the foundation of their new chapel, and he hoped the day would come when they would be able to rejoice not only that they had finished the chapel, but that they had commenced and finished their Sunday schools. No church was complete without a Sunday school. They were the nurseries of their churches and if they could only lay hold of the rising generation and train them up in the principles of the Baptist denomination, they would not have many youths who would be able to say that up to 15 years of age they knew nothing of the principles of the Baptists. (Hear, bear,) He proceeded to remark that the success of a church lay in individual effort, and urged the tmem to be earnest workers. The meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks

div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE CASES.

SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. ASSAULT WITH A POISHR.—A HAPPY FAXILY.—Binny Hines was charged with haviog unlawfully assaulted her husband, Thomas Hines, on Thursday.—Defendant pleaded guilty to " hitting him with the poker." From the state- ment of the Chief Constable it appeared that complainant had his son before the Bench on Thursday, for assaulting hint, and he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment. The defendant was then heard to threaten her husband, and they quarrelled as they left the police court. In half an hour afterwards the complainant -returned to the police station with his head bleeding and stated to Mr. Hunt that his wife had been "using" the poker. The woman was apprehended, but admitted to bail in the evening, and as the husband did not now appear to sustain the charge, Mr. Hunt thought they mnst have "made it up."—Defendant said she had not seen him or been near the house since.—Mr. Hunt remarked

_ that some time ago the son was given a good thrashing by a policeman at the request of the parents and next morning they appeared before the Bauch awl bald the officer had not given him half enough. (Laughter.)—Mr. Burgess (addressing defendant) : I don't believe in a woman using the poker and if your husband had been here you would not have got off so easy as this.—At this point complainant ap- peared and said he did wish to press the case if she would be better.—Defendant: I have ten children by this man and was never in prison before. He has hurt me much worse than that and I never brought him here. Many ablack, eye have I wore with that man.—Defendant VW ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months in one surety of 15 ; but she refused to accept her husband as a surety saying she would have nothing to do with him. TILEFT.—George Morton, a young lad; was charged with stealing a 'quantity of bottles from the premises of James Toole, marine store dealer, Rylands-street. Three other youths, whom the police had been unable to apprehendovere implicated in the charge and the prishner therefore was re- manded until Tuesday and admitted to bail. A POST OFFICE OFFICIAL FINED FOR ILLTREATINO PoNY.—Joseph Dean, postman, was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a pony and cart in Buttermarket- street at 5-30 on the previous day, and also with furious driving and cruelly illtreating the pony.—P.C. Neill said he observed the defendant, with three other persons in a cart drawn by a pony at the time and place named. Defendant held thereins and was flogging the pony, which was going as fast as it could, With the whip. Perspiration was dropping from the pony's belly and it was in a wretched state.—Defendant asked the Bench to deal leniently with him as he had a wife and ten children.—He was fined ss. for being dru_nk, and 108. and costs for the furious driving and illtreatment of the pony, total £1 4s. 6d.—Alderman Chandley severely censured the defendant and said ha ought to be ashamed of himself for spending his money in, getting I drunk when he had a family such as he stated. MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere),, Alder- . .

elan Burgess, and Co,uecillor Fairclough. NEGLECT OF FAMlLY.—William Farrell, labourer, was charged with deserting his wife and time children on the 20th March. Mr. Harbourne, the relieving officer, said 285. had been expended in relieving defendant's family, Prisoner made .a statement as to his having been out of employment, but he had now obtained work. He would, however, have to leave it to join the Militiaeand he would pay the money on his release. The case was, therefore, adjourned for five weeks.—Martin Miskell, a farm labourer, was charged with deserting his wife, who thus became chargeable to the War- rington Union. Mr. Harbourne Bahl the prisoner's earnings for the last month bad averaged Ti. 9d. per week. Prisoner's two sons were before the Bench on Friday to ehow cause why they should not support their mother, but as prisoner was in work the case was dismissed. The, Mayor: You cannot get money out of a stone. Mr. Harbourno said the Guardians had had much trouble with prisoner, who was a very bad character, and who was drunk in town on Satur- day. His wife had had relief all the winter. Mr. Hunt handed up a 'character "' sheet, from which it appeared prisoner had been often before the Bench for various offences. Mr. Feirclough elicited from the prisoner that, in addition to his wages, he got his food. The ease was dis- missed, the Mayor remarking that it was one where the Guarcliane wanted the prisoner committed, and they could, not go into the circumstances. It appeared that the prisoner's average earnings were voey little, and if the Guardians had asked for an order the Bench would have favourably considered the matter. A "MODEL" TEBTOTALLER.—DanieI Connor, an old mar, WAS charged with being drunk and riotous in iuttermarket- street, on Saturday night.—Mr. Hutt observed that this wee prisoner's 40th appearance, and that be had only reaently been committed for two months for theft.—Prisone7 stated he would sign teetotal if the Bench would let him go.—Mr. White drew from the man an acknowledgment that he had previously signed the pledge nine times.—As Mr. aunt did not press the charge, prisoner was discharged. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.-3ohn Bibby aria fined ss. and costs for being drunk in Mersey-street D 7•4. Saturday night, and assaulting P.C. Seed. HEARTLESS. ROBBERY. Thomas Shaw, plasterer, was charged with stealing 7d. from Margaret Hickey, a girl nine years of age, on Saturday night.—The girl was sent by her mother to the Lower Angel public-house for a pint of beer and a quart of vinegar. She gave up her bottles to the man serving at the counter, who went into the cellar, and the prisoner, who was standing at the bar asked if she had paid for the beer. Being answered in the negative he said "Give me your money and I will pay him when he comes up.' Tusun- suspecting girl delivered up her money and ' prisoner immediately walked out. When the man returned from the cellar, the girl commenced to cry, and said a man bad taken her money. A discription was given to P. C. Monaghan, who captured a yolth answering that description, but the girl and waiter said It was not the man. Subsequently he apprehended the prisoner who„was at once identified as the i thief. Prisoner n answer to the question where& heweuld be tried by the magistrates present orby a jury, said by a •urv.—The case was therefore remanded until Tuesday. 3 MOTHER AND DAUGHTER SENT TO PRISON.--Margaret Mallonev (12), was charged with stealing a pair of boots, a picture, looking-glaee, and a number of other artieleeQt the

value of 225., from the dwelling house of Joseph Croker, furniture dealer, Dial-street ; and Mary Mahoney, her mother, was charged with receiving the same knowing them to be stolen.—Margaret pleaded guilty and the mother not guilty. --The" girl it -appeared, ball fdr a month worked as a servant with Mrs. Croker during the day, returning home to.steep every night During that time she had missed a number. of articles, and entertaining suspicion of the servant questioned her. The girl denied all knowledge of the articles, but a pair of boots disappearing on-',Saturday night, Mrs. Croker on Sunday , morning threatened to send, for a policeman if the girl did not confess her guilt, and she then admitted. stealing the boots which she had pledged at Jacksen'efor is. 9d. Mrs. Croker went to Werth Mra: Mahoney, but the door was locked. ,She. thereupon looked.through the window and discovered several articles which she had missed lying about the house—Mrs: Croke identified the Majority of the -articles Produced as her property.--P.C. Cox deposed to finding the articles produced in prisoner's house. When charged Mrs. Mahoney said her daughter told her that Mrs. Croker had given the-articles to her, and she was to pay 6d. per week. She was .not aware she had stolen them.— Councillor Fairclongh Can your girl read and 'write? Prisoner: No.—Mr. White said she had been twice fined for ef sending lide to' scliool. The prinoner Margaret was Sen- tenced to a fortnight's imp.risonmentand five years in a re- formatory school; and Mrs. Mahoney for a month with hard labour: • , Tr:mine-Y.—Before Alderman Webster; and' 'Councillor' - 'Broadbent.' ' A QuauTErra.QF YOUNG Tninve.s. George Morton, Albert -Massey, Walter Triddell, and John Kelly, were charged with stealing a quantity Of bottles, value 34 from -the premises of James Toole, marine store dealer, Rylands- street, on Thursday. P. C..Clynes was passing up Rylands- street, when he saw three of the prisoners reaching bottles ,from under the doer of Toole's marine stores. On seeing' the officer the lads each picked up a bottle and ran away'. P. C:r Clynes returned and found Morton, in the stores.--All the, boys with the exception of Morton pleaded guilty; Morton stating that he had never handed any bottles 'to the boys outside. •They, toned upechalfpently which-had to gobs and it /ell to him. He stated-Massey had handed the,. bottles to those outside.—The boys were ordered to receive six strokes each with the birch`rod. THE HEARTLESS ROBBERY FROAri LITTLE Grm....-Thos. Shaw, a young man was brought up on remand Jcharged with stealing 7ad. /tom a girl named Margaret Hickey, on, Saturday bight. When before the ' Bench on Monday,' he elected to be tried, at Liverpool; but now-said he would be tried , by ,the magistrates prasentand pleaded not guilty.— P.C. Monaghan stated that when he apprehended the prisoner he said; "Ididn't take it." Take what?" halted the officer. "What you're bringing me for," was the reply:--Prisoner was committed to.gaol for one month, with hard labour. A MrsraxEs" MILITIAMAN.—WaIter Harrison, a strong looking youth, was charged with being a deserter from the 3rd King's Own Staffordshire Militia, having absented him- self from training this year.—lt appeared prisoner had pre- sented himself as a recruit to the regular army on April sth stating that the militia did not assemble until the 6th, but on the authorities applying to the militia for his release, they claimed him as a deserter,-as the training had commenced in February.—The Bench thought prisoner had made a mis- take in the date, and senteneed him to a day's imprison- ment.

A DESERTER.—Henry Burke was charged with deserting from Her Majesty's ist battalion of the ' Bth Foot, at Man- chester, on the 6th Mareb.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and-he was ordered to be handed over to the military escort, which. was in waiting. Manfilbey.—Before Captain Litton and Councillor Fa . a irclough. PCIDLIC-11011811 Fnacsi.--Charles Roherts *at charged with unlawfully assaulting Elizabeth McCormack, on Satur- day, and Tbomas McCormack was charged with assaulting' Mary Bridge.—Elfzabeth McCormack said that about five o'clock on Saturday afternoon an altercation occurred in the Red Lion public-house between the two prisoners about some money which hicgorinack owed Roberts. Mary Bridge than entered, and, ' saying she had " wanted '! Mrs. McCormack a long time seized her by the hair, of the head,' thumping her Al the while." Prisoner Roberts then went to separate them, but "only struck McCormack." Mrs. Roberts stated !` Cush "knocked her senseless on the floor.—Many witnesses were called on each side, one stating that Mrs. Bridge ins getting the best of the fight, and McCormack struck her, but that Roberts was fighting with another man outside.—The case against Roberts was dis- missed, and McCormack was bound over to keep the peace for six months.

Thin&Dicr.—Before Captain Litton and E. Milner, Esq. Vacnresey.—,John Smith, of no settled abode, crag charged with vagrancy. Hose and Crowa-street, at 12-30 that morning.—P.C. Lawrence having proved the case, the Chief Constable, in reply to Captain Litton, said the prisoner was a Warrington man. He vras a good workman as a Sadler, and had got rid' of a good deal of money. This was the fourth time since February last that the prisoner had been charged with vagrancy. The prisoner had onry just come oat of prison, and as the Bench said he seemed to like going to gaol, they gave him another month. INDECENT 13EHAYtouR.---liebecca Bate, a woman of loose character, for being drunk and guilty of indecent behaviour in Dolman's-lane, was fined 20s. and costs, or one month. —The Assistant-Clerk: Are you going to pay It? Prisoner: I will pay it in Walton when I get there. NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

LECTURE AT NEwrox.—An interesting lecture on " Mada- gascar and Its people "was delivered, in the Congregational Schoolroom, on Wednesday, by the Rev P. (1- Poaher. The lecture was well illustrated by a number of Malagasy curiosities, and on Thursday the various curiosities and articles of native manufacture were sold. The proceeds are to be devoted to the fund for the support of native teachers and evangelists in the Island of Madagascar. ST. PETER'S CHORAL CLASS.—The members of thig class celebrated the close of the season by holding a tea party and ball in thle Town Hall, on Monday evening. All passed off in a very enjoyable manner, dancing being kept up with spirit until the wee hours of the morning. ' CONCERT AT NEWTON. A miscellaneous concert was given in the Town Hall, on Thursday evening, by the mem- bers of the St_ Peter's Singing Class. Mr. Joseph Owen acted as conductor, and Miss B. Mayor as accompanist. The programme was fairly rendered. NEWTON Liam—Notwithstanding the morning rain on Good Friday the lake was largely patronised, and the whole fleet of boats were in active use throughout the (lily. Satur4 day also was a busy day; but on Monday several plc-the. parties visited Newton from Liverpool, Bolton, aid surround- ing districts, and the attendance was very large. Nnwrox GUN CLUIL—The members of this club met on Saturday last, the day was ail. that could be desired, and the attendance was large. Several important events were shot off for, cups given by Members, and the silver challenge cup of the club. Geed scores were made. The champion cup was. won, for the second time in succession, by. Mr. R. Stone, who killed his first 11 birds, whilst Mr. Williams missed his eleventh bird; the cup now becomes the property of Mr. R. Stone.

EARLESTOWN VESTRY MEETING.OLI 'Monday evening the annual vestry meeting for passing the accounts and election of Officiirs for the ensuing .year was held in the vestry of St. John the Baptist Church, Earlestown, the Rev. T. R. Matthews vicar, presiding. The receipts for the year amounted to £202 7*. 4d„, and the payments to £205 Ss. ad. Messrs. James Fairclough and Francis Harwood resigned, their office of churchwardens. and Mr. N. Slinn and Mr. T. Nevitt were appointed. Phis sidesinen elected were Messrs. Fairclougb, Harwood, Corlett, Owen, Scott, Pennington, Jackson, Molyneux,,,,and Kirkwood. A voluntary rate of 2d. in the pound was muted. WARGEAVE \TEN= MEETING.—The annual meeting of 'Emmanuel Church, parish of Newton, was held on Tuesday. Tile Rev. John Whitley presided, and amongst. those present were Messrs. W. Thompson, T. Hunt, Peake, Tootal, Shaw, Davies, sen., Eimber, -Catterall,. -Davies, jun., Haselden, Ballatc. The accounts for the past year,after being audited by Messrs. T. Haielden and W. Johnson, showed that .£l3B Itis, '9d. had been received, and -2132 4s. Oct. expended, leaving a balanceln hand of za 12s. The following officers. were elected for the ensuing year :---Wardens, Mr. W.. Thompson and 'Mr.. T. Hunt; sidesmen, Messrs. Tootal„ Peake, Shaw, Davies, Siarkie, Bate, timber, and Catterall. A. voluntary rate of 2d. in the pound was carried on the motion of Mi. Kimber seconded by Mr. Tootal. The usual allowances to the eb:dr, organ blower, choir master, and organist were passed , unanimously - The churchwardens were ippoitited, repreeentitiveg to the Diocesan Conference on the motion of Ms: Peake, seconded by Mr. Catterall. A .resolution was passod to prevent parties from trespassingand loitering about the church yard dining divine worship. The Rector read &letter front the Bishop,per Dr. Hume, asking for a religious census throughout the diocese, and he intimated that he intended complying-with the request of the Bishop. The proceedings terminated with the usual vote of thanks to the Chairman. and past officers.

SALT —Tbe large shmmen, ts for the, month of TRADM March have stiffened the markets materially, and with the active Spring demand for the trade it is expected the prices will rise. Brine is beginning to be low again and coal is not very ahundant. Prices for the latter material, are fully oce shilling above those of last Christmas. By comparing the total amount exported from the Mersey during the month ;with the amounts, say fcom 1875, during the same period of the Tear, one may see bow the trade prospers—for year 1875, 51158; 1876, 74,605; 1877, 71,159; 1878, 76,156; 1879* ggseg; 1880, 63,27154: but this year it is 92,142 tons. Goon Farnmr ex.'Wutsurbrin.—This has always beat a great day with the pang people cormeoted with the United Methodist Free Churches. They, for weeks before the day, are preparing either to recite or sing for the hundreds, who assemble to see and hear them. Being a dull and windy day, the Sunday richOol could not procession the streets. This, with singing at various places, they did on Sunday instead. Having been regaled with buns and coffee, &c. on Friday, the business of the evening, under the presidency of the superintendent of the circuit, was commenced, and like a" marriage bell" all went well; Messrs. J. Hulse apd J. W. Bennett, the prompters, having little or nought to do. The pieces and singing of the young people gave every satisfaction. Miss Buckley accompanied the mon the organ and likewise the choir, when during the collection they sang an anthem "Come unto me.".- The High-street chapel was well filled.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN-z. The first meeting of the newly-formed Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday-, when there ion present the Rev. Cancn Barclay, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. T. Norms'), W. Whittaker, W. Handley, W. Fisher, H. Neild, R. Ashton, J. Knowles, J. Challoner, P. Percival, J. Campkin, A. Broady, W. Pickering, H. Lowe, J. Derby- shire, J. Mclntyre, J. Highfield, C. Mounfield, T. Massey, and H. Linaker (clerk.)
ELECTION OF CILAIIIMAN. The CLERIC produced the certificates of the returns of Guardians and the nomination papers for each township, and remarked that the first business was the appointment of

chairman. Mr. Mc-INT./Its had very great pleasure in asking the Board ' tare-elect their worthy chairman Canon Barclay. He was an ' oldtried gentleman whom they hadhad presiding over them for some years. He had filled the office with the greatest ability, and they had, he was sure,watched the business tact which the rev. Canon had brought to bear upon the duties a the office. The manner in which he had presided over this Board rendered Canon Barclay pre-eminently fitted, to his mind, to continue to preside over them; and he had great pleasure in proposing the re-election of the Rev. Canon Barclay. Mr. ROBERT AsnTolt seconded the proposition. He was sure no one could have carried on the business better than the Canon had done during the past few years. (Hear, hear.) Ho had been a member of the Board for some 10 or 12 years, and during the whole of the time he must say the Rev. Canon Barclay had acted as chairman in the most becoming
11121113er. The proposition was put by the clerk, and carried unani-

The Rev. Canon Barclay then took the chair amidst applause. He said to the mover and seconder of the resolu- tion he felt highly indebted, though he felt the remarks that been made of him were due perhaps rather to the warmth of personal friendship than any merits of his own. To those who constituted the last Board he felt very much indebted, because he con- sidered their re-election of him to the chair was equivalent to a vote of confidence, and showed their approbation of his conduct in the past. He took the first opportunity of thank- ing them for the vote of thanks passed on the last Board day. To the new members he also returned his thanks that they had followed in the wake of the older members who had tried him, and he trusted had not found him wanting. Ile only hoped and trusted he would merit their approbation in conducting the business of the Board in such a way as would secure him a similar vote if necessary at the end of the year. For many years past th 3 Board had been a model to many of the Boards in the neighbourhood for the courtesy with which the members had behaved one to another, and for the unanimity which was characteristic of their proceedings. If they had had a little difference during the past year it was only what might be expected when so many gentlemen met together. But they agreed on many occasions to differ, and there was no reason why a difference of opinion should prevent courtesy one to another if not mutual friendship. He always thought anybody had a right to use their influence at this Board, and even if the majority mtght not agree with them, it was their duty, as Guardians, to bring forward anything they thought necessary for the public good; and he hoped they would always have a fair and patient hearing. He did not think it was at all neces- sary to impute evil or secondary motives to the persons with whom they differed; and if, in the heat of debate, a gentle- man made a strong statement which might not be perfectly in accordance with truth, it was not necessary that they should consider him as having gone beyond the bound of truth and call him names, but that they should consider it a mistake such as they were liable to fall into. He hoped, during the year, that they would see the proceedings of the Board conducted with that courtesy which should be shown by one gentleman to another, and that they should give him credit for good motives even if they differed from the opinions of their friends and neighbours. APPOINTMENT OF TICE-CHAIRMAN. Rev. J. W. N. TANNER said the vice-chairman, who was nominated some years ago, had served them well and given entire satisfaction to the whole Board by the way he had conducted the business in the absence of the chairman. He, therefore, had the greatest possible pleasure in proposing Mr. John Ashton as vice-chairman. He believed Mr. Ash- ton was the only member who had not been absent once during the past year, and he was therefore thoroughly en- titled to occupy the vice-chair during the ensuing year. They were happy to say their chairman was very seldom absent, but when he was Mr. Ashton ably occupied the position. Mr. PICKERING seconded the resolution, which was carried without dissent. Mr. Asirrort, having taken the vice-chair, thanked the Board for having re-elected him. He said it had always been a pleasure to him to attend the Board. The business was always conducted with unanimity, and it was a pleasure to preside over such a body of gentlemen. FINANCE COMMITTEE. Mr. Norman said the Finance Committee bad that day passed accounts amounting to £2BO ss. sd. MASTER'S REPORT. The Manua (Mr. R. Jones) reported that there were 157 inmates in the house as against 158 in the corresponding week in last year. Of 18 vagrants relieved durieg the week 14 were men and 4 women. In attendance at the Workhouse school there were 21 boys and 29 girls; and 12 boys and 21 girls were receiving industrial training. Oat-door relief had been administered to 702 persons at a cost of £62 Os. 2d., apportioned as follows: Runcorn, £34 38. 9d.; Frod- sham, £I4 Os. 6d.; Budworth, £l3 165.; as against 677 persons relieved in the corresponding week in last year at a cost of £65 12s. sd. --------

_ THE EIIRIAL OF PALTERS AT RUNCORN. The CLERK read the following letter which had been re- ' ceived from Mr. W. F. Seikold, secretary to the Runcorn Burial Board :—"ln further reference to my former letter, dated March 1, and to your reply thereto, dated March 21, 1881, I am instructed to inform you that cases have been brought under the notice of the Burial Board of the relieving officer having refused to order the burial of deceased persons in unconsecrated ground, and that for your information I beg to enclose a notice of interment given by the relieving officer for the burial of the body of James Ford, the friends of whom wished the corpse to be interred in the Roman Catholic burying ground, and so expressed their desire to the relieving officer before interment. I have received no com- munication from you upon this subject since the meeting of Guardians, to which you refer in the concluding paragraph of your letter. P.S.—Please return the notice for interment after perusal "—A second letter was received frem Mr. Sal- keld, as follows :--I have received a note from Mr. Coleburn asking me to send to you a copy of the form of receipt I give to the relieving officer, and others, upon payment of fees at this office, wlaich is enclosed herein. I also send :a copy of the regulations, fees, and charges of the Burial Board, think- ing it may possibly be useful as a reference. I beg to state that the fees due to the Dissenting ministers, and to the Roman Catholic priests are paid to them immediately after each funeral; those to Canon Barclay are retained in my pos- session to the end of each year (by his desire), and then paid to him, and a short statement of the accounts of funerals, headstones, monuments, tic. is rendered also." The CLERIC said he did not see what the Board had to do with the matter, because the account appeared to be paid direct by the relieving officer to the secretary of the Burial Board. _ .

Mr. NORMAN : It is paid all in one sum. The Crarux Yes; so it appears. There is nothing at all about fees in this sort of receipt. I don't quite see how Mr. Wright directed the body to be buried in consecrated ground if the friends have desired otherwise. Mr. Norm/art That is the question. But I think the Chairman named it at the last Board meeting, and gave, as I told them at the last meeting of the Burial Board, a very fair challenge for Mr. Wright to try one case. I think you said 20 years ago yos tried a case, and brought it before the auditor. If Mr. Wright did the same thing again, then you would try it before the present auditor. The CHAIRMAN : Yes. He appealed, he said, to the auditor, who would have surcharged, it he had not waived it, for all fees that Mr. Wright had paid to Dissenting minis;..ers, OR the ground of a certain clause in the act of Parliament Which said the fees were to be paid to the person who had hitherto been accustomed to receive them. As no one had been accustomed to receive fees for burials, there having been no barials at the time he accepted the vicarage of Runcorn, he was entitled to the fees. Of course Mr. Wright inferred from this that the interment must take place in consecrated ground. He gave it as his opinion that there was no necessity for it to take place in consecrated ground; but as guardians of the benefice of Runcorn, and of the patrons of Christ Church, Oxford, and as a matter of principle, which they heard so much about, he should claim the fees. The CLERK said as to the fees in that account he did not see what the auditor would have to do with it, because fees were not mentioned there. Mr. Wright got a receipt of the interment of the body in the cemetery. He took it that it would be for the Burial Board, and the clergy to fightit out between them. If the relatives of the deceased person expressed a desire that the body should be buried in uncon- secrated ground he did not see how Mr. Wright had any con- trol over them. The CHAIRMAN: This control is, I believe, the inference drawn from the decision of Mr. Kyffin Roberts, the Govern- ment auditor. The CLERK : These orders may have been made since Mr Roberts's decision. The CHAIRMAN : Although we hear so much about prin- ciple from certain members of the Burial Board, they want the fees; they may say what they like. The CLERK said Mr. Wright ought to be distinctly given to understand from the Board that he must carry out the Local Government Board orders in reference to the burial of the dead, and if a person in receipt of relief had expressed a. desire before dying that he should like to be buried in a cer- tain plaits, or if a relative expressed a desire after death, he should carry out that desire. Mr.II.O4DLET said they could take advantage of an act of Parliament that was passed in the year 1857, whereby the Guardians had power to make arrangements with any burial authority for the burial of poor persons, whether they were paupers at the time of death or persons who could not afford to pay for the interment. It would be a wise thing, he thought, if the Board wrote to the Runcorn Burial Board and entered ir..o a contract with them for the burial of poor persons and let the fees be paid direct by the Board. The CLERK : They are novr.
