div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 23, 1881.

-- An important inquest was held by Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, a the Grapes Inn, kept by Mr. Ormesher, Halton- road, Runcorn, on Wednesday morning. Mr. Wm. Richard Earp acted as foreman. The Coroner, in opening the proceedings, said the case was rather a peculiar one; and he thought it was, perhaps, only right that he should give the jury a bare outline of the facts. So far as he knew up to that time, the deceased went, in company with a woman named Emma Jones, employed at the Bull's Head public-house, Halton-road, to Frodsham on the afternoon of the 17th inst. As they were returning home, and between Halton Station and the village, the de- ceased complained of not feeling well, and told the woman to walk on a little in advance and he would overtake her. She did so and, after waiting a considerable time of de- ceased, who did not make his appearance, she went back to look for him in the plantation which he had entered. She found him, and he complained of being seriously unwell, but added that he thought he should be better shortly. She waited for deceased between one and two hours, and, as he did not seem to get well, she went to an adjoining farmhouse and asked for some assistance. The farmer's wife, to whom application was made, said that if the woman could not get any assistance, and Jones did not get any better, her people should help her. He believed that the woman did not visit the same house again, but she met a farm labourer, to whom she spoke, and he went with her to look at the man. His visit led him to think that Jones had been taking drink, and that as soon as he had had a little sleep he would be all right. At the earnest request of the deceased, the woman Jones went home, as it was getting late, and he thought he should soon be better. Before leaving him she took off her petticoat, wrapped it round the deceased's head, and put him into as comfortable position as possible. The woman returned to the Bull's Head, Halton - road, and told her master and mistress what had happened. On the following morning she went back to the plantation, and found deceased in the same position as that in which she had left him. Shp found a police officer, who had him carefully removed home, but he died shortly after his arrival there. The Coroner bad had a post mortem exami- nation made of the body by Dr. Carruthers, junior, and no doubt the evidence of that gentleman would guide them very clearly in coming to a decision as to the cause of death. Of course, their primary duty, as a jury, was to enquire into that cause; but it would also be quite proper for them, under such circumstances, to consider whether there was any blame attathing to any one.— Edward Jones 7 Bold-street, Runcorn, a jeiner, identified the body as that of his father. Deceased had been living in lodgings with a man named Allen Hewitt. He was a blacksmith, and he last saw him alive on Saturday after- noon, at the Old Quay works. He had always had good health though of late he had complained a little about his head. He might add that he did not see deceased on the Monday.—F.C. Lowndes, stationed at Halton, said that on Monday morning he went to the Hallwood farm, and saw a man of whom he inquired where he should find deceased. He was shown to a plantation, between Halton station and Halton village. He then found deceased, who was gasping for breath, and in a dying state. He felt at the man's hands and feet, which were very cold. He then went to Gorst's farm, and, with the assistance of two gamekeepers, put him in a conveyance, and took him to the surgery of Mr. Car- ruthers, senr., at Halton. The doctor tried if deceased could swallow some brandy and water, but be could not. Mr. Carruthers told him to take Jones to his lodgings and put bottles of hot water to his feet. They adopted these measures, but they did not appear to have any effect upon deceased, and he died in about an hour and a half after his arrival home. He did not speak after being found. From enquiries which he I made at the Hallwood and other farms in the neighbour- hood of the plantation, it appeared quite true that applica- tion had been made by some one on the Sunday night, to have a man removed in a conveyance.—Emma Jones, the woman referred to above as being in service at the Bull's Head Inn, Halton-road, was then called. She was respect- ably dressed in black, and in answer to the Coroner's questions, said she had at present no fixed place of abode. On Sunday morning, as she was cleaning the lobby, near the front door, her master came down and said she was to make I haste and get breakfast. There had been an agreement en- tered into when she took the situation, to the effect that the mas' er would get breakfast on Sunday mornings, and she said "Aml to get it ready The mistress then came to the top of the stairs and said something, but she (witness) made no reply, as she wished to finish her work at the front door, because she did not like to be seen scrubbing there when people were going to clapel. She had notice given on Sun- day morning that she was to leave "because she stayed over the time when she should have been in, owing to remaining with poor William." [Witness appeared much affected.] She then deposed that her real home was at Copperas-hill, Ruabon, and she was a general servant. She knew deceased some years ago, and on his entering the Bull's Head about a week after she had come there she recognised him. On the previous Sunday afternoon be came for her, and asked her to go a walk with him to Frodsbam. They bad nothing on the way to that place, but when they got there they had a glass of ale and an orange each. On their way home, and when between Halton station and the village, he asked her to go on and he would overtake her shortly. He was such a long time that she went back, and found him crouching down, with one band upon his forehead, vomiting. She held his head, and said, "Oh, William, whatever is coming to you ?" He said it was quite possible the orange he had eaten had had something to do with making him ill, and he thought he felt better as he vomited it. °lt would be about five o'clock when he went into the plantation, and eight when she left him there, previous to which she took off her flannel, wrapped it round his head, and did everything she could to ' make him comfortable. Witness next described how she had visited several farmhouses in the neigh- bourhood with the object of getting assistance. She offered to pay for conveyances to take Jones home, but the people made various excuses. At one place she said she would put the horse into some kind of conveyance they had, if the mistress would let her, but she replied that there was no one at home, and she could not permit her te do so. She next went back to the planta- tion and found deceased sleeping naturally and quietly. One farm labourer, who .;ould be called as a witness, went to look at him. She should not have left Jones but he pleaded with her to do so, saying "My dear girl,l have love for you as for my own girls. Go, my love." Deceased also put before her the possibility of losing her month's wages if she did not go home. On leaving, Jones kissed her chcek

and shook her hand, and remarked "I shall be all right just now, and be up in the morning like a lark." She should certainly have remained with him if she had any notion he would not get better. When she get home it was nearly closing time—about ten minutes to ten o'clock. On enter- ing the house her mistress came out of the parlour, and she told her in what a condition she had left Jones. The mis- tress replied" Oh, I will not have this sort of work; stopping up this time of the night." She again told the mistress how the poor fellow had been taken ill on the way home, and that at last she had been obliged to leave him in the planta- tion in order to return. The landlord then came to her and said to his wife, "You go away; I will take her in hand now! You shall have your money and go about your business." She did not say much in reply, with the excep- tion of the remark that she should expect her month's wages. Her master also told her that the character she had d given him was a false one, but she indignantly denied this impu- tation, and said she was prepared to go with hip to a man who occupied a respectable position in the neighbourhood, i and prove the correctness of what t stated. On leaving deceased,wit h her afterw h when nc esnhseul lasttin withgsaw o jtnhees,f ashr dleacbioduedr e tk r twhoe h was watch and any money he had upon him with her, fearingi that some one passing by might be tempted to rob him. On the Monday morning she wished to find thel person with whom deceased lodged, but she I had considerable difficulty in so doing. After much trouble she discovered the place, and asked deceased's " boy " if his father had gone to work. She, then, for the first time, became acquainted with the fact that the poor man had not returned home. • She went straight back to the plantation, and found him in the same position as she had left him. She next went for the police and a doctor. It never entered into her head to go to the police on the Sunday night and tell them that deceased was in the wood. She did not knew the neighbourhood well, and was much puzzled to find some of the houses. She had never been out with deceased before, and on Sunday be said he had never had anything amiss with him until the pre- vious three or four days, with the exception of some dizzi- ness in the head. Deceased had promised to call and see her several times, and on coming to the house on the pre- vious Sunday, she told him that his promises were only like pie crusts—made to be broken. Deceased said he had not called because of late be had been troubled with head ache.—ln reply to the deceased's son, —a young man about twenty-two years of age— witness said Jones did not ask her to call at his lodgings after she got home on Sunday night. She asked him several times where he lodged, and he said, "Never mind, for you will not find it if I tell you." In reply to the keeper of the Bull's Head public-house, who was present, witness said he did not tell her, on going home on Sunday night, that if she had left Jones in that condition she had better "look after his requirements."—The pnblican told the jury that he did not believe the statement of the witness as to deceased being so poorly, or he would have taken his trap and brought him home, "for he was a very harmless man, and a frequent visitor at our house."—By the Coroner: Witness said she had been in Runcorn one month. Mr. W. H. Carruthers said he made alpost-morteet exami- nation of deceased on Tuesday. There were no marks of violence or injury. The luegs were full of a dark fluid, and the heart in a state of fatty degeneration. The liver was enlarged. shewing symptoms of commencing disease. The I stomach and intestines were healthy, and nearly empty. I The other organs were healthy. He opened the head, found a! large clot of blood, and extensive extraversation of blood at the base of the brain, which was the immediate cause of death, which resulted from what was commonly called apo- plexy. He could not say whether the apoplexy com- menced before the exposure or not. Deceased had symptoms of apoplexy coming on—pain in the head and congestion or the brain—and instead of any proper measures being taken to relieve him, he had been subject to this ex- posure in the wood all night, when rupture of the base of the brain would probably commence. He could not, how- ever, really say when the artery gave way, which caused the apoplexy. The exposure might have brought on the apoplexy even if he.. had i not been ailing before. There was no trace of poison n the bqdy.— By Inspector Hollingworth : He had attended deceased for bronchitis some 12 months ago, and had always considered him a broken down subject. A labourer, named John Coomes, of the Hallwood-farm, gave evidence as to the woman Jones cominz to the farm for a conveyance, and going to the place where deceased was lying. He was pre- sent when she took deceased's money, and she then said she would go for a cab. He remained up to about 12 o'clock at night, but she did not return, and then he went to bed.— By a Juryman: He advised the woman to get a cab but he was under the impression that deceased had had drink and would come all right after he had slept. He told the woman that she could get a cab at Halton Castle Hotel. It would be about twenty minutes past eight o'clock at night when she first fetched him.—The Foreman of the Jury thought that P.C. Lowndes ought to be coniplimented for the course he took on being told the deceased was in the plantation.— The Coroner: Yes, I think he did all he possibly could.—A Juryman: If the man and woman who knew he was in the plantation had taken effective steps, the result would have been very different. Another Juryman : I think the officer should be recom- mended to head quarters for his bisection in the matter.—A Juryman: It was his duty.—The Coroner: There is a great deal of satisfaction in feeling that one has done his duty.— The Foreman: Yes, and it is also very satisfactory to know that when you have done your duty, your services are appreciated! It is not very nice when you do your best and never even get thanked for it.--The Coroner, in summing up, said he very much doubted whether, in law, there was any blame attached to any one for the action taken in the matter. The, woman Jones appeared to have acted up' to what "light" she possessed.—The jury returned a verdict of " Died from apoplexy."

taken steps to place your affairs before the Local Govern- ment Board, so as to obtain the sanctions necessary to cover and ammd the irreg,ularities which led to these difficulties. As far as the audit on which • I am now reporting is con- cerned, I was not in a position to take these sanctions into account, as I am of opinion that they cannot be held to be retrospective; and I was, therefore, compelled to disallow the interest paid on all the money borrowed in excess of your powers and sanctions. My comprehension of the com- plications and difficulties to which I have alluded was very much assisted by the statements prepared by your chair- man, and his explanations thereon, and I wish to express my acknowledgment of the attention and assistance he rendered me at the audit." The CHAIRMAN said that the overcharges consisted of a great number of small items, which it was perfectly certain would be sanctioned by the Local Government Board the minute they were laid before them. It was not necessary that he should read through half a dozen pages; any of them who wished to do so was at perfect liberty to inspect the documents, which were upon the table. The items were merely things of very little consequence. , No further discussion took place upon the matter. AMUSING ATTACK ON QUERN-STREET. The following communication was read The Lindens, Haslingden, Lancashire, April 20th, 1881.— Gentlemen,—l have some property in Queen-street, Widnes, which is in a shocking state of repair, and absolutely tenant- less. I wish, If possible, to alter the state of things. I am prepared to spend some little money in putting the property in a tenantable state qf repair, if there is a prospect of being able to get tenants. lam informed by several Widnes people that the very name of Queen-street is quite sufficient to prevent any improvement in the district. (Laughter.) My request to you now is to alter the name of the street; and, as far as I am con- cerned, I will try, by respectable tenants, to keep an imp, eyed appearance. If you would kindly change the name--(much laughter)—to any of the following—Osborne, Prince's. Bal- moral, or King, or any other name you may think proper, I shall be extremely obliged. (Renewed laughter.)—With kind regards, gentlemen, believe me yours truly, THOMAS MLR- °MAYES, Captain 2n(l. L.R.V. The CHAIRMAN said he should certainly object to changing the name of the street. Why should they take away the name of the Queen from the street P (Loud laughter.) Let Mr. Hargreaves get his property put ir repair. Even if the Board were wishful to meet the request of the writer of the letter, it would be an awkward matter, and lead to much mystification, as the name Queen-street had now been placed in a large number of legal conveyances. The subject then dropped, and the business of the Board terminated.

div.head: – _ WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: - _ WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of this Board was held on Thursday. Major Cross occupied the chair as returning officer, and there were also present Messrs. O'Keeffe, Handley, Kershaw, Knight, Gossag.e, Carlile, Carey, Brown, Pankhurst, Hayes, Gaskell, Oppenheim (who acted as law clerk pro. tern.) Beasley, Allen (accountant), and Higginson, surveyor.

ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. Mr. CAREY moved that Major Cross be re-elected chairman, on the grind of the amount of work which he had done dur- ing the past year, and the success that had attended it. Mr. CARLILE, in seconding the motion, said they would remember that it was understood amongst the members of the Board, that Major Cross should be re-elected to the office until the incorporation of the town, when he was to be the first mayor. (A. laugh;) I The resolution was passed unanimously, and the Chair- man thanked the members for their continued confidence.

FILLING LP A VACANCY. Mr. CAREY proposed that Mr. Thomas Shuttleworth be appointed to the vacancy on the Board, caused by the death of Mr. Robert Barrow. Mr. Shuttleworth was one of the candidates brought forward at the late election by the Rate- payers' and Owners' Association, and he thought it would be an act of courtesy to appoint him to the post. Another point in his favour was that he belonged to the same end of the township as the late Mr. Barrow, and was a very able man, who had plenty of leisure, and was in a position to render the Board considerable service. Dr. 0' KEEFFE seconded the motion, on the ground that if the proposal was supported, it would be a graceful compli- ment to the Ratepayers' Association. - Mr. KNIGHT supported the proposition. Mr. BROWN had not a word to say against Mr. Shuttle- worth's abilities to fill the office, but he thought that the usual course on such occasions had been to appoint the gentleman who was found to have received the highest num- ber of votes amongst the defeated candidates. This gentle- man was Mr. Samuel Sadler, and he had pleasure in propos- ing him. The CHAIRMAN said, that as no one else appeared willing to second the nomination of Mr. Sadler, he would do so. The votes were then taken, and there were for Mr. Sadler —the Chairman, Mr. Pankhurst, and Mr. Brown. Against —Messrs. Carey; Heyes, Gaskell, O'Keeffe, and Knight. The last-named gentlemen also voted for Mr. Shuttleworth at this stage of the proceedings. The Cum-Imm; : The proposition in favour of Mr. ' Shuttleworth new becomes the substantive motion. Mr. KERSHAW proposed another amendment, in favour of the election of Mr. John Houghton. Mr. CAULILE seconded the motion, and caused some laughter by remarking that if. they decided to adopt a " fresh-blood " candidate, they would not offend the sup- porters of either Mr. Sadler or Mr. Shuttleworth. There voted for Mr. Houghton—Messrs. Brown, Carlile, Kershaw, and Pankhurst. The resolution in favour of Mr. Shuttleworth was then put as the original motion, and carried. IMPORTANT REPORT FROM THE AUDITOR. The CHAIRMAN read a report from the Local Government Board auditor, which stated that he had completed the audit of the accounts for the year ended at Lady Day,lBBo. The following are the particulars of the rate presented for audit, viz. :—Arrears brought forward, £436 is. 2d. ; rate laid July 22, 1879 £8,060 7s. 9d.; total, £8,496 Bs. 11d.; collected, £5,598 169. 7d.; balance carried forward, £2,897 12s. 4d. He called attention to the very large amount which appeared to be overspent on the rate account, and recommended the Board to make every effort to meet the yearly expenditure, by levying sufficient rates to cover it. They would see from the general order for ac- counts of Local Boards that it was essential that all items of expenditure should be carefully kept to their proper account, and that one of the principal objects of the department is that the amounts borrowed for specific objects should be ex- pended for the purposes for which the loan is sanctioned, and that the expenditure of one loan should not be mixed up with that of another, or used for general expenditure. Mr. Darlington added—" It may hardly be necessary to refer to the deputation of ratepayers who attended the audit, as many of the members of your Board were present, and you are fully aware of the nature of the objections which were raised to certain items in your accounts. I may state simply that I gave the gentlemen who. attended the audit every opportunity of expressing their views, and, after con- sidering the objections they took, and the explanations which were given by your chairman and clerk, I fcund it my duty to make certain disalbrances, the particulars of which, and my reasons for making the same, will be found in your general, gas, and water ledgers. It is only clue to your Board that I should add that many of the financial difficulties which were presented at the time of the recent ' enquiry by Mr. Harrison, have teeu overcome, us you havq

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—B2foro Mr. F. H. Gossage. BLIND BUT LIVELY.—Thomas Mack, a blind man, who had been apprehended by P.C. Laing for causing a disturb- ance in Water-street, and breaking several windows in a dwelling-house, was ordered to pay the costs and find sure- ties for his future good behaviour. - -

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sen. (chair- man), and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A. POLICEMAN.—John Evers, an Irish man, employed as a chemical labourer, was charged with being guilty of a breach of the peace in Waterloo-road, and assaulting P.C. Laing.—Complainant gave evidence to the effect that on Saturday night, at quarter past eleven, the defendant and about 50. other men were making a ter- rible disturbance in Waterloo-road, and insulting people as they passed. He went to the place in company with P.C.. Graham;and asked the men to go away. Prisoner struck him in the eye with his fist, and he was afterwards knocked down. On getting to his feet he saw about 12 men kicking P.C. Graham, who was on the ground, and stonea and bricks tieing about. He and the other officer had to use their staves in order to clear the street.—P.C. Graham gave cor- roborative evidence, and added that he was also knocked down and kicked by several men as be was seizing a labourer named O'Neill.—Mr. Husband appeared for the defence, and called Michael McCann, with whom flip prisoner had lodged for several years; Michael Currigan, Ann Mc- Cann, and John Evers, to prove that the pri- sioner was in McCann's house during the row.— The Chairman said the Bench believed the evidence of the officers, and defendant would be fined 40s. and costs for the assault. The breach of the peace summons would be dis- missed. . THB CASs OF ALLEGED SUlClDE.—Bridget Oates was i again brought up on a charge of attempting to commit . suicide. The particulars of the case have already appeared in our columns. Prisoner was discharged on promising not

to offend again. CHARGE OF STEALING CLOTHlNG.—Elizabeth Ann Wads- worth (14), was charged with stealing wearing apparel, value 55., the property of Francis Cook, Pool-street, some three months ago. Prisoner was taken in by the prosecutor, as she had no home, and she had acted as cook. During the time of her stay, though she admitted she had been well treated, prisoner stole the articles.—Mr. Gaskell said the Bench did not like to commit the girl to prison, and they agreed to discharge her on condition that she was given up to some respectable relatives, who live in Warrington,

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes (chairman) and Mr. R. M. Brooke. A " BRUTAL " BOATOWNER.—Richard Clayton, boat- owner and carrier, was charged by Elizabeth Cox, the wife of a man in his employ, with savagely assaulting her on the 11th inst.—Complainant, who appeared with her head cut, said she did not wish to go on with the case, as the prisoner had a wife and family.—Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, said the prisoner had been apprehended on a warrant, which had been applied for by her, and she must give what evidence she had to offer.—Complainant said she was in the Swan beerhouse, Shaw-street, when the prisoner seized her by the hair, threw her into the street, and kicked her several times. She was hurt very seriously, and applied to a magistrate for a warrant.—The Chairman said the Bench considered this a very serious case. Prisoner was a gross, brutal fellow to abuse a woman in the way he had; and, not content with dragging her into the street by the hair, he had deliberately kicked her. They should not allow the case to be withdrawn, but should fine him IN and the costs £1 138 10d, or in default of payment 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour. TEE Jocirra's ADVENTURE: FALLEN GREATNESS.— Thomas Carroll and Francis Hughes were charged with begging at Weston.—Joseph Gaiter, quarryman, said that about six o'clock on the morning of Saturday he met the two men, and Carrol asked him "if he could give them a bit of weed." He said he could not, on which they begged for "a copper or two," with which he also declined to pro- vide them.—P.C. Cooper said he apprehended the prisoners at the Prospect Inn. He asked them where they came from and they said, "We have no come from," On asking for from, names prisoners said they had none.—The:prisoner Hughes was discharged, as it was not proved he bad begged. The man Carrol denied having begged, and called upon heaven to witness the truth of his statement. He added that he was a jockey, and formerly rode for the Earl of Stamford and Warrington. He won the Chester cap in "two seconds."—Superintendent Williamson said he had known the prisoner for many years, and his was the old, old tale of ruin by drink.—The Chairman said Carroll would have n fine and the costs (8s) to pay, or be sent to gaol seven days. ALLEGED BREAKING INTO A BOATMAN'S HOUSE.—Ann Wolfenden, Richard Barker, Ellen Coffey, Margaret Smith, I alias Jones, and John Smith, all well known characters, were charged with breaking and entering the dwelling-house of IWilliam Moreton, on the 13th inst., and stealing a bed quilt, a quilted skirt, a dress, a brooch, a scarf, and two pieces of I crotchet work. Prisoners were also charged with receiving the same, knowing them to be stolen.—Mary Moreton wife of William Moreton, boatman, Hankey-street, said that on the 7th inst. she left her house for the purpose of going with her husband in a boat. She made everything secure before going away. The catch on the kitchen window was fastened with a piece of wire, and the articles which the prisoners were charged with stealing were all right. They went to Sowerhy Bridge, near Halifax, and returned to Runcorn on the 14th inst. On going to the house they found that the blind of the kitchen window was down, though it had been left up. The catch of the window had been forced open. On going upstairs she missed the articles mentioned in the charge.—John Powell, engine driver, employed by the Bridgewater Navigation Co., said he lives next door but one to the prosecutor, and his wife asked him to look after the house whilst they were away. On the 13th init. he saw the place safe and about two hours after, from what was said to him by his son, he went to thehouse again, and found that the window had been broken open and the blind removed. The wire by which the window was fastened had been taken away.—Michael Callighan, a lad aged 13, of Back Brunswick-street, said that on Thursday, about noon, he went to Harper's-brow, in Water-street, and saw the prisoner Coffey, who gave him the petticoat and asked him to go to Mr. Lomax's pawnshop in Church-street and get as. (M. upon it. The pawnbroker refused to lend the money, and kept the petticoat.—Mr. John Arthur Smith (occupying Mr. Lomax's late shop), said the quilt produced I was brought to his place of business by the prisoner Barker, and he lent him 2s. upon it. On Thursday the last witness brought the petticoat to pawn, but he refused to advance the money, and told the police. Coffey came up about the petticoat, and' stated that it was her own and she had bought it from a woman at her house. Mrs. Jones afterwards came to the shop, and said the skirt was Coffey's; and she and Coffey produced two pawn-tickets purporting to affect it. The dress skirt was pledged on the 13th inst., by the prisoner Jobe Smith. who stated that it belonged to a boat- man lodging at their house. He lent them 4s. lid. upon it.—P.C. Hibbert said that on the 14th instant he went with Sergeant McMichael to Lomax's pawnshop, and apprehended Coffey and Jones. That morning he had taken Barker into custody at Weston, and, in reply to the charge, he said "It is all right. I heard that you had been after me, and I was coming to give myself up this morning." Barker also admitted having been to the pawnshop with the quilt. Prisoner, Smith, on being taken into custody, gave him a brooch, a scarf, and two pawntickets.—Sarah Withington, female searcher at the police station, said that on proceeding to inspect the clothes of the prisoner Coffey, she said it was no good going to the trouble, se she had nothing. She found 4s. ncl., wrapped in a paper, concealed in Coffe's bosom. The woman told her it was money she had saved, and witness might keep it, as she did went any one to know she had it —Sergeant McMichael proved the apprehension of Smith and Wolfen- den.—Each of the prisoners made statements in reply to the charge. Wolfenden alleged she had given 14s. 6d. for the things on the fairground, Manchester; and Mrs. Jones said that on the previous Thursday Wolfenden came to her house and asked to be allowed to wash her. She permitted her to [do so, and gave her a cup of tea. The various prisoners alleged that they had accepted most of the things to pawn, ' and some of them to keep, on the understanding that they ,had been bought at Manchester.—Each of the prisoners was committed to the Quarter" Sessions for trial. POOR RATS.—Mr. James Robinson, assistant overseer, applied to the Bench to sanction a new poor rate of 13d. in the for Anton-by-Sutton, to realise £!40; and one for Aston Grange at is. in the £, to realise about £s3.—On the application of Mr. Gorst, of Sutton a poor rate cif lid. in the L, and estimated to produce MO& is. 2d., was granted. —ln answer to the Bench, Mr. Gorst stated that the rate was the lowest in Sutton of any township in the union. TrinsnAT.—Before Mr. William Banks. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON AN ITMSD FARM LABOURER—Martin Towey, farm labourer, was oharged with having, on Stinday the Bth August, 1880, malltiously wounded Michael Bones, by stabbing him with a knife.—Complainant saiar that in August test he was working at-Mr. Lowe's, Sutton hall, and at the same time the prisoner was employed at Bradley, near Frodsham. On the night of the day mentioned, complainant was at Frodsham Bridge publichouse in company with the prisoner and a number of other men, six of whew names he gave. They left about two o'clock, and as soon as they got outside the prisoner quarrelled with some Englishmen, and sai&he would fight any of them. Complainant and his friend went on, but they had not got far when Towey and some of his companions Came up and said) that they had received a thrashing near the publichouse,and they intended to punish Bones and' his friends for not staying to assist. ,them. Near the turn-bridge John Towey, one of the. prisoner's set, kicked and struck complainant. The latter and his two companickns got home to their shanty as soon.as they could, with the object of closingAhe door, but the-op- posite party rushed against it. John Bones was struck on the head with a bottle and a number of cans. Three of the men gt upon John Bones, awl complainant went to them to pull them away. He begged there not kill John Bones, and immediately afterwards he managed to get away. Four of the men then set upon him (complainant), got him down, kicked him, and beathim ashen} as they could. Thoprisoner had a taile in his hand, and as he held it in front of him, said to complainant "A will do your bit now I have you." Prisoner made several stabs at his face and neck, once on the forehead, and once on the left ear. Whilst the prisoner was ding this, the other men were holding him. Several men came to complainant's assistance, and he got away, but found he was badly injured. John Bonea gas corroborative evidence.—Dr.McDougall said be examinea the complainant on the 9th Augnst. His face waks ejrumid with dry blood

div.head: WIDNES MILTON_ CONGREGATIONAL
div.p: WIDNES MILTON_ CONGREGATIONAL

CHURCH. The annual tea partjoin connection with Widnes Conn- gational Church, was held on Wednesday. After tea an interesting public meeting was held. Mr. John Hough was voted to the chair. During the evening the choir rendered several pieces in a very effective manner. The CHAIRMAN expressed his regret that the attendance was not larger, but said this was probably attributable to the bitter north-west wind then blowing. A statement as to the church funds would be in their hands within the next few days, which would show that they could say they owed no man anything. (Hear, hear.) This, he considered, was a very creditable result in the case of a church which was not very strong in numbers. He urged the members to develops the voluntary principle in the young who were connected with the chapel, and he was sure that if they did so they would be pleasantly surprised at the result. He hoped they would cultivate a personal interest in the success of that place of worship. The Rev. J. D. THOMAS, of Runcorn, hoped that all present were trying to help one another in the Christian life by increasing each others spirituality, praying for one another, and endeavouring to be present in the House of God as frequently as possible. He concluded by expressing his feeling of affection to Mr. Peters, the pastor, who preached at his ordination service. The Rev. T. TISSEYMAN (Wesleyan) dwelt upon the necessity of self denial, which was the soul and spirit of Chtistianity. The Saviour taught it, and where there was , true self-denial there would also be zeal. The sublimest r, illustration of self-denial which the universe ever saw was I spoken of in the words of the Apostle, "Who though He was rich, yet for your sakes became poor, that ye through His poverty might become rich." This sublime fact was inscribed on the firmament of humanity and written upon every page of the moral history of our world. Let them go to the stable of Bethlehem, and there they had one of the most splendid illustrations of self-denial which the angels ever say. Could they tell the distance between the throne of God and the manger at Bethlehem? There were vast distances which might be measured, but this distance was immeasuratie' inconceivable, unutterable! If they studied the lives of the grandest men who ever lived, they would find they were men of self denial. As instances of the development of this faculty, he referred to St. Paul, to John Williams, the famous missionary of the South Sea Islands; John Howard, the philanthropist; and Elizabeth Fry. It was said in the scriptures that the world should be filled with the glory of God, as the waters covered the sea; and he believed this. (Applause.) The Rev. Jovor YONGE, of Warrington, said he supposed and believed that the sondition of the commercial world during the last few years had told upon them in Widnes like other people, notwithstanding that a great statesman, who had just passed away, told them some time ago that chemicals were rising. He was sorry to hear that chemicals in some quarters had gone down. Difficulty, however, let it be as great as it might, was not a thing which ought to frighten a man. What a magnificent illustration was given to them of the power there was in nature to overcome diffi- culties in the history of that remarkable person whose death was now upon everybody's lip! Certainly no other stge had ever seen any one man who, in his own individual life, more magnificently illustrated the power to overcome diffi- culties than did Benjamin Disraeli. When he began his public career, everything was against him ;—all social forces were against him. Disraeli, to begin with, was a man of an alien race. He bad no wealth; only a very few—a com- parative few—influential friends; and yet that man, with his alien race, his social disabilities, and the al most unimaginable obstacles with which he had to contend, set before himself the aim of making himself a name and a place in this country and the world; and he supposed that no man had more succeeded in this century than the Earl of Beacons- field. Beginning in obscurity, he died the other day almost one of the most marvellous men in the present century. I Even from the life of the late Premier, Christians might learn the lesson that difficulties ought not to depress or dis- courage, and certainly not to defeat them. Even though there might be difficulties in connection with that church, yet he W ished them to remember, as a brotherhood of Christian people, that prayer to God and devout faith in Him must, in the long run, succeed. The most successful church they could find in that or any other country could never have been made what it was unless it bad laeen sup- ported by praying and earnest deacons and other officers. Without these, no minister in the world could make a church succeed. The speaker next referred to the fact that he happened to be district secretary for the County Union in that part of the county, and so he wished them to know that the members of that body were steadily decreasing the grants to places which had already been helped, as they could not possibly carry out their chief object—which was to open out other places—except the stations already helped became self-supporting. Mr. Yonge concluded by expres- sing the deep sympathy which he had with Mr. Peters in the great personal troubles through which he had been called upon to pass since coming to Widnes, and saying he hoped their pastor was finding sympathisers amongst them, so that he might feel that he and the members of his church held one another in individual esteem for Christ's sake. On the motion of the Rev. THOMAS Privies, seconded by Mr. Sitirrmtwonvir, a vote of thanks Was passed to the speakers, the choir, and the ladies, who had provided tea.

div.head: FRODSTIAM.
div.p: FRODSTIAM.

- - - EASTER AT FRODSRAM.—The holiday season i$ Considered to have fairly commenced at Easter, and this year has been no exception, although on Good Friday the number of visitors was not so great as M former years in consequence of the very unfavourable weather. The pleasure grounds on Overton Hills were, however, well patronised, and Monday being a fine day and Bank Holiday, some hundreds poured in by road and rail to review their acquaintance with rural^ scenes, and, hail the advent of balmy spring which is showing itself in the bright sunshine, bringing out the leafy buds and making nature look gay. The political contest now being waged caused the town towear an unusual lively appearance owing to the various tiagsand banners displayed by each party. A cutting east wind on Monday tended somewhat to mar the pleasure of the visitors, but with "Youth at the prow and pleasure at the helm," it did not seem to make itself felt, other thao to suggest a return home at a more reasonable hour than would have been the. case had a more genial wind, prevailed.

TIRE Marra) Ronan NAIL. COMPANY, Lnurst2.—l will be seen from the prospectus of this company, which appears in our advertising columns, that the company pur- pose raising a capital of £200,000 in 200,000 shares of £1 each, 133,334 shares being now offered for publie aubscrip- Ition. The company has been formed to carry into effect the !union of the Acme Horseshoe Nail Company, Limited (Whipple's Patent), and the European Globe Nail Company, both established for the manufacture of finished horseshoe nails by machinery, under patents and trade marks, for Great Rritain, the whole of Europe, and the colonies. £130,000 of the capital is already placed, haying been issued fully paid to the shareholders of the Acm6 Horse Shoe Naik Company, Limited, and the European Globe Nail Company. With Whipple's machines finished horseshoe nails, with any shape or kind of head, can be produbect, including every- thing, at 2 1-16 d. per pound. Horseshoe nails are now sold at prices varying from sd. to 7& per pound. Each of Whipple's patent machines can produce in ten hours 600 pounds of nails, and it Ds esti- mated that a profit of at least £.15 as, per ton will accrue. The company have acquired a going profitable horsiness with a large and increasing connection, and a well-known and protected trade mark.. The establishment of a factory to use Whipple's machines is in progress at Milwit, and will be worked In conjunction with the factory of the Horse Shoe Manufacturing Company, Limited. Meanwhile this com- pany will have about 20 tons of finished nails per week ,made at the factory at Gothenburg to work the trade with, upon ; which a profit a £4OO I),er week ya at once assured,

Mr. HANDLEY said he knew the form of receipt, and he thought if it was looked carefully into they would find it gave a receipt for the fees that were mad to the Burial Board, and that the fees were received and paid entirely out- side the Burial Board accouflts. lie thought be was correct in saying so. There were two members of the Burial Board present, but be knew, having examined the balance sheet of the Burial Beard for some years, there was no statement whatever as to the fees paid, except it be in a line how much had been paid by three classes Churchmen, Dissenters, and Roman Catholics. He believed during the past fortnight Mr. Wright had refused to grant burial fees to the parent of a child that died in Runcorn, because they would not take it into the consecrated ground. The parent very properly refused to take it into the consecrated ground, because the father of the child was buried in unconsecrated ground, and as the brothers subscribed for the grave it was only natural that the mother should desire it to be buried by the father. There was nothing for it, seeing Mr. Wright refused to grant the fees, but to go about collecting the money. The brothers again came to the aid of the mother, and the child was buried in its father's grave. He thought it was rather a disgrace that one of their officers should put people to the necessity a going up and down to collect. It appeared to be very hard hearted to want to separate the father and child in death. Mr. Wright said he could only give an order for burial in the consecrated ground, but he was con- vinced he was wrong. He thought the relieving officers should be provided with orders to give the fees. That would deal with the case entirely. The Cumulus said it would not settle the question be- cause it referred only to the payment cf fees direct to the Burial Board. Somebody bad remarked that the payment Of the fees to ministers was quite outside the Burial Board. Mr. HANDLEY said it was not for the Board to fight the question. He thought the Burial Board ought to be, and are competent to deal with a question of that kind without it coming there. They had their ewn opinions on the matter, but he thought his suggestion would be a satisfactory way out of the difficulty. Mr.Wnicurr was called in and explained the case to which Mr. Handley bad alluded. Mr. HANDLEY: Whom do you pay the fees to Mr. Waiont : I pay them te the secretary. Mr. Hat/DLIT : Do you get a bill of them? Mr. Wain= : I get a form of a bill and receipt. Mr. HANDLEY : And are all the fees entered that you pay? Mr. WRIGHT: Yes. Mr. HANDLEY : It is simply a payment to the Burial Board, and not to the vicar or anyone else. I think the Act says the fees are to be paid to those who have been accus- tomed to receive them. The fees have been paid ever since the cemetery was opened to the Burial Board, and I don't think anyone has received the fees except through the

secretary. The CHAIRMAN said it was simply an arrangement with Os secretary. He had told them what was the simplest way to get out of the difficulty. If Mr. Wright paid the fees to anyone else he would appeal. Mr. HANDLEY declined to deal with the matter in that way. So far as the Board was concerned, they ought te have an arrangement with the burial authorities, and then Mr. Wright would have nothing to do but sign an order and send it to them, and they would charge the Board. After some further discussion, it wa.l decided, on the pro- position of Mr. HANDLEY, and seconded by Mr. ROBERT Asicrox, that the Burial Board be written to in reference to an arrangement for the burial of poor persons dying in Runcorn.

MR. BAXTER'S RETIREMENT. A letter was read from Mr. Thos. Baxter acknowledging the receipt of a letter from the Board containing the resolution passed at the last Board meeting, and expressive of regret at Mr. Baxter's retirement. THE MASTER'S FAMILY. Mr. LOWE gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that inasmuch as Mr. Jones's sons were now in busi- ness, a fresh arrangement should be made as to the main- tenance of his family. This was all the business.
SAD DEATH OF "RUNCORN MAN.

Over the left ear there was a clean-cut wound three-quarters of an inch long. The inner side of the left ear was cut half an inch, to the bone. On the top of the head was a cut one and a half inches long, down to the bone' and on the back of the cranium another wound five-eighths of an irkch long, which penetrated to the bone.—lnspector Hollingworth proved receiving the prisoner into custody at Sallaghaderreen on the 11th inst. Prisoner said that if he had known that the affair had not been settled he should have gone to America.—Towey, in defence, said that on the date of the alleged assault he had only been in England three weeks. He professed to have been badly assaulted himself during the struggle which took plaoe.—He was committed to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT. TRURSDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. SINGULAR ACTION AGAINST A LANDLORD.—Bennett /J. Walsh.—Mr. Hamilton, tarrister, instructed by Mr. Alfred Harrison, appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. Mattinson, barrister, instructed by Messrs. R. Davies, Sharp, and Kirk- connel, for the defendant.—Mr. Hamilton said this action was a claim in replevin by which plaintiff sought to have it declared that certain goods, which had been distrained, were his property, and that defendant had no right to distrain. It seemed that defendant, Mr. James Walsh, was the owner of some property in Kerfoot-street, Warrington, and that the plaintiff and his wife had, some time previous to the month of April, 1879, been carrying on a small provision shop in Winwick-road. In the month of April plaintiff's wife re- ceived a call from defendant, who told her that he had a vacant shop which she might take with advantage. Defen- dant made several calls, and ultimately induced her to take the shop; and as an additional inducement told her he was in a position to advance her a sum of money to enable her to stock the shop. It was agreed between defendant and plaintiff's wife, in the plaintiff's presence, that this shop should be taken, and that Mrs. Bennett should have a loan of £2O from defendant. That arrangement was carried out, and he could not say that plaintiff had not made himself responsible for that debt, because there could be no doubt he had ratified the contract made by his wife. The arrangement was that plaintiff was to pay 85. a week for rent and 3s. for interest en the loan; and he was instructed that, from the commencement of the tenancy down to the time the distress was put in, the arrangement had been carried out strictly— that was to say, payments had been made at the rate of lls, per week during the whole of that time. No receipt was given for the money; hut on the 31st January, 1881, Mr. Walsh called and told Mrs. Bennett he required a bill of sale on the shop property to secure the £2O which he had lent two yeare before. Mrs. Bennett declined to do anything of the kind without consulting her husband. Plaintiff also declined to give a bill of sale, and defendant was told they would not give one. Then for the first time defendant pro- duced frorehis pocket two rent books, and said "Very well, , then you had better take your rent books." The first of those rent books professed to be a rent book for the year 1880, and commenced in a very remarkable way with "due, one year's rent, £2O 16s. Od." That was on the 3rd May, 1880, and there was a pencil receipt for Bs. rent, nitialled by the defendant. All the remaining enteries on the page with defendant's initials, were in ink. He would hand to his honour the rent books, and ask him to conclude that they were a carfully prepared concoction delivered on the 31st January, this year, and not delivered at the time the entry purported to be made. He asked his honour to look at the ink in which the entries were made. It was a remarkable coincidence that the first entry was in pencil and that all the ''remaining entries were in ink, gradually becoming fainter as they got to the bottom of the page. Plaintiff had regularly paid the stipulated rent and 35. interest upon the loan, and it was not until Mr. Walsh found that he could not get a bill of sale that he produced the rent book which he had carfullv prepared beforehand to saddle these people with. He was told that before Mr. Walsh delivered thet rent book he had been in communication with Mr. Winskill, the gentle- marl who conducted the distraint proceedings, and he should challenge his friend Mr. Mahtison to put Mr. Winskill in the witness-box, in order that he could cross-examine him to see whether he was not the person who suggested the infamous device. The rent was not due; and if his Honour came to the conclusion that the payments in the first year were made on account of rent and not on account of loan, then he sub- mitted he would be entitled to a verdict for the plaintiff. If they believed the story told by the plaintiff's wife that she had paid Bs. a week rent, and 3s. interest during the whole of that year, it did strike one as a very remark- able thing that, if she was paying off the loan during the year, Mr. Walsh should be allowing the rent to remain , The whole thing bore the impress of a clever dishonest person contriving to impose upon persons who were illiterate, and scheming to enable him to get a bill of sale over the pro- perty.—Plaintiff's wife was then called, and confirmed Mr. Hamilton's statement. She said she had no rent book given her when they went into possession. They had paid Ils. per week-Bs. for rent and 35. for interest. 17p to the 3rd May, 1880, there was no rent due. It was not true that de- fendant brought a rent book on that day. She continued from that time up to the day the distraint was made to pay the rent and interest regularly. On the 31st January de- fendant reduced the interest to 2s. a week. After that time she paid Sc. a week rent and 2s. a week interest, and at a quarter to two, on the lit of March, paid him £3 12g., all the rent she owed, but an hour afterwards the distress was put in. She could not read writing, but could read figures, and she thought the £2O entered in the book was for money they owed for the loan. She never asked defendant to put the Bs. a week to liquidate the loan.— 'Cross-examined : They went into the shop on the 21st Atari!, 1879, and the £2O was paid to them a week before. They made the first payment of interest on the 13th May. She always paid the money herself, but never asked for a receipt, as she had so much coufidence in defendant. She never had a receipt. It was not arranged between defendant and her husband that the latter should give a promissory note for the £2O. It was not a fact that when she paid money she took a paper upon which defendant entered the amount of the money she paid. Defendant did not say about the 3rd May, 1880, she was to pay the rent regularly. She had bad the bailiffs in the house before this distress, and had sold part of the furniture, but she had always given the money to the defendant.—Plaintiff said he did not give his wife authority to obtain the £2O as a loan, but be knew of it afterwards, and allowed her to pay the interest. He had seen sums of 11s. a week paid. He never saw the rent' books produced up to the time the distress was put in.— Thos. Randle Bennett, labourer, Chapel-yard, said he took possession of the property on the instruction of Mr. Winskill. While he was in possession defendant eame to the house, and Mrs. Bennett said she did not owe him the money for rent; she owed him kr borrowed money, and if he had sued her she would have acknowledged it. Defen- dant said he did not care about borrowed money, he wanted his money.—Mr. Mattinson, in opening the defence, stated that there was undoubtedly a very serious conflict of evi- dence, and the duty was cast upon his honour to determine upon tkat conflict of evidence whether lur could' believe plaintifror defendant. His learned friend opened with a charge of the gravest character against defendant. The accusation amounted to nothing short of this—that Mr. Walsh, in order merely to accelerate his 'legal remedies against these persons, entered into a conspiracy of the foulest character, in conjunction with Mr. Winskill, an auctioneer of this town, and on the suggestion of Mr. Win- skill concocted false books, and proposed that day to palm off the false books upon the court, and by that means ob- tain an undue advantage against these persons. So far as the accusation affected Mr. Winskill and defendant, he should put Mr. Winskill into the box, and he would tell his honour there was no foundation whatever for that suggestion. Very naturally he would suggest in the ordi- nary course of his business a distraint for the rent due, but he had no personal acquaintance with plaintiff or defen- dant. He certainly never made any suggestion of the description stated, and throughout only acted in the ordi- nary course as an agent to make a distraint. If that were so his honour would conclude that the case for the plain- tiff, apart altogether from the discrepancies in the evidence, was considerably painted by the fact that it was put upon such ground• that if his honour held in favour of the plaintiff he would practically be passing the gravest con- demnation both upon defendant and Mr. Winskill. It seemed common ground that on or about April, 1879, plaintiff did become: the tenant of this shop, also that a rent, of Bs. per week was agreed to, be paid for the shop, and a loan of £2O was made by Mr. Walsh to the, plaintiff. Defendant had for some time been acquainted with the mother of plaintiff's wife. He looked upon her as a worthy woman, and was disposed to deal fairly and kindly with the plaintiff when he entered the shop. At that time plaint:ff was a person of little or no means, and' it was necessarytif the business was,to be a suc- cess, that some small capital should be advanced. Defen- dant undertook to advance £2O, and at a very early period of the relations between them intimated that: he would be content, go far as regarded the rent, that it should lie over for some time and get into arrear. The suggestion made on the other side on this point was one which he was instructed to say was void of foundation, and, as to the interest, only 5 per cent. was to be paid upon the £2Ol The suggestion that there was a sum of 3s. a week paid by way of interest was utterly untrue. Defendant saw the wife, and asked her to give him an acknowtedgment which it had been arranged the. husband should give on account of the loan. Mrs. , Bennett made a difficulty on the ground that her husband could neither read nor write, and did not like to put his name on paper. Inconsequence of that, difficulty, defendant said he would not force them to fulfil the promise, but they must commence to make their payments. All the money ihe would give them credit for and. deduct it from the loan, I land for the present they could allow the rent to go on. The 'reason defendant adopted this course was obvious. Defen- dant felt so long as there was still stock and furniture on the premises he could distrain at any time he saw the plain, tiff getting into difficulties, and there was likely to be smash. From April, 1879, to May, 1880, plaintiff's wife came to defendant with small sums of money, for which, be gave her credit. At the outset defendant gave Mrs. Bennett a bill on a sheet torn from a copy:book. That paper, he would prove, was seen in the possession of the plaintiff. On deducting from the £2O the sums paid dur- ing the 12 months, together with interest at sper cent., defendant found a balance against plaintiff of £6 18s 6d. Defendant then said to plaintiff's wife it was time they com- menced to pay some rent, and he gave hoe the first of the two rent books. The first entry upon the book was the amount of arrears £2O 16s, and he would swear he gave thero the book on the 3rd May, 1880. There was no doubt ever Since the 3rd May, until a short time before the distraint took place, the plaintiff had paid pretty regularly the rent due, but he had never liquidated the balance. He submatr.4 the plaintiff had not made out his oase.—netsudaut sa'S

• HARMSTON'S NEW CIRCUS, SANKEY-STREET, WARRINGTON. Open every Evening at 7-0, commencing at 7-30. MID-DAY PERPORAtANCE, Wednesdays and Saturdays at 2-30. Enthusiastic reception and continued success of the pretty Scotch spectacle THE GATHERING OF THE CLANS, Performed by 50 little girls, dressed in Highland ceaume. Their Military manceuvres, patriotic songs, choruses, reel of Tulloch, sword and shield exercises, gun and bayonet exercises, lc., are the admiration of every person. MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice Ire Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing and Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass.
